units.title: Welcome and Onboarding: Start Here
units.summary: See the shape of your year, learn how each week works, and set up your portfolio so you can start strongly.

p: By the end of this welcome unit you will be able to:
Explain the aim of the year and the six pillars you will build
Describe the weekly Learning Loop and how you will be assessed
Set up your portfolio and make your first commitment to the programme

Welcome to the One-Year Life Skills Academy. Every Saturday for fifty weeks you will build the character, communication, thinking and future-readiness skills that no exam can fully measure, through true stories of young people from around the world, honest discussion and projects you actually create.

There are no high-pressure written exams here. You grow by showing up, practising, reflecting and building a portfolio of real evidence. Think of this year as a gym for life skills: you get stronger only by doing the reps.

b: Learn: build a skill each week
Lead: use it to lead yourself and serve others
Impact: prove it with a project that changes something

p: Quarter 1, Personal Excellence (Weeks 1 to 12): mindset, self-knowledge, confidence, values, goals, time, emotions, habits and resilience. It ends with the My Future Blueprint capstone.

Quarter 2, Communication and Leadership (Weeks 13 to 24): clear speaking, listening, storytelling, body language, teamwork, conflict, negotiation, service, networking and culture. It ends with The Leadership Challenge.

Quarter 3, Innovation, Thinking and Digital Readiness (Weeks 25 to 38): critical and creative thinking, problem solving, decisions, ethics, project management, leadership, AI and cyber safety. It ends with the Innovation Challenge.

Quarter 4, Career, Money and Impact (Weeks 39 to 50): financial literacy, entrepreneurship, design thinking, careers, CV and interviews, etiquette, community impact, mentoring, and your Grand Capstone.

sections.h: How each week works: the Learning Loop
p: Every unit follows the same loop, because we learn best when we experience, reflect, understand and then apply.
1. Learning goals: know what you are aiming for.
2. Warm-up and true story: connect with a real person facing a real challenge.
3. Think about it: discuss the story and what it means for you.
4. The big idea and the method: learn a clear idea and a simple step-by-step tool.
5. See it in action and common mistakes: watch the method work and avoid traps.
6. Practice lab: try it with a partner or on your own.
7. Reflect and quick check: write in your journal and test your understanding.
8. Weekly challenge: use the skill in real life and add evidence to your portfolio.

b: About 60 minutes per unit, live with a facilitator or self-paced
The quick-check questions are practice only and never count as an exam
The weekly challenge is where the real learning happens

p: Vision: to raise confident, ethical, emotionally intelligent and future-ready young people who can lead themselves, influence others positively, solve real-world problems and thrive in school, university, careers, entrepreneurship and life.
Motto: Learn. Lead. Impact.
Core values: Integrity, Respect, Responsibility, Excellence, Empathy, Courage, Innovation, Leadership, Collaboration and Lifelong Learning.
Assessment is 100% project-, portfolio- and participation-based. There is no written exam and no 100-question test bank.

Your evidence comes from four sources: weekly participation and challenges, the portfolio you build all year, three Quarterly Capstones (Weeks 12, 24 and 38) and the Grand Capstone and Summit at Week 50.
You will earn Bronze, Silver and Gold digital badges and fill in your Future Ready Passport as you go. Capstones are judged with a rubric that rewards growth, not just polish.

b: Showing up and taking part honestly
Real evidence of practice in your portfolio
Reflection: what you learned and what you will change

p: Show up on time and ready to take part; each session matters.
Respect every voice in the room. Put-downs, mockery and interrupting are not accepted in discussion or role-play.
What is shared in reflection stays in the room, unless someone's safety is at risk.
Do your own work: portfolio pieces, weekly challenges and capstone contributions must be honest efforts.
Give feedback kindly and receive it openly. Growth, not perfection, is the goal every week.
Start a folder (paper or digital) with these sections and add to it every week:
Weekly reflections
Monthly projects
Leadership activities
Presentation slides
Certificates earned
Community service record
Goal tracker
CV
Personal mission statement
Final capstone project

Write your name, your reason for joining and one thing you hope to change by Week 50
Pick an accountability partner who will check in on you each week

units.title: Week 1: Orientation: Becoming Future Ready
units.summary: Understand what 'future-ready' means, map your six pillars and write your starting line for the year.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Explain 'future-ready' in your own words and name the six pillars of the programme
• Rate yourself honestly on each pillar and pick the one you most want to grow
• Write a Letter to Future Me that you will open at the Week 50 Summit
'If you could master one skill instantly, what would it be, and why?' Go around the room/call.

sections.h: True story: Tanmay Bakshi (18 years old) (Toronto, Canada)
p: Tanmay Bakshi spent his childhood playing with computers just like other kids played with building blocks. By the time he was just five years old, his dad taught him how to write very simple computer code. While his friends were playing video games, Tanmay was busy trying to understand how those video games actually worked under the hood. He did not want to just use technology; he wanted to build it.

When he was 11 years old, Tanmay heard about a brand new technology called Artificial Intelligence, or AI. Instead of waiting until he was an adult to learn it, he decided to start studying it right away. He ran into countless bugs and errors that made him want to pull his hair out. He often sat at his desk for hours, typing away and laughing at his own silly coding mistakes. But he kept adjusting his skills because he knew the world was changing fast, and he wanted to be ready for the future.

By the age of 15, major global tech companies noticed his unique skills. They invited him to speak on huge stages in front of thousands of adults to explain how the future of technology works. Tanmay proved that you do not have to wait until you grow up to prepare for the future. By starting early and learning the skills of tomorrow, anyone can become ready for whatever changes the world brings.
What does 'future-ready' mean to you, in your own words?
Tanmay didn't wait until he felt qualified — where in your life are you waiting to feel 'ready enough'?
What is one skill you want to walk away with by Week 50?

Being future-ready does not mean predicting the future. Nobody can say which jobs, apps or crises will matter in 2040. It means building a toolkit that keeps working whatever arrives: character, communication, clear thinking, digital confidence and money sense.

Schools test what is easy to test. They rarely test how you handle nerves, disagreement or failure, yet those skills decide who thrives in an exam hall, an interview or a friendship under strain. This programme exists to train them on purpose, one Saturday at a time.

b: Future-ready = a flexible toolkit of skills and character that keeps working when the world changes.

sections.h: The method: The Six Pillars Snapshot
p: 1. Pillar 1, Personal Excellence: knowing and managing yourself (mindset, goals, habits, resilience)
2. Pillar 2, Communication and Relationships: listening, speaking, teamwork and handling conflict
3. Pillar 3, Leadership and Influence: leading yourself first, then others, through service
4. Pillar 4, Innovation and Problem Solving: thinking critically and creatively to solve real problems
5. Pillar 5, Digital and AI Readiness: using technology safely, smartly and ethically
6. Pillar 6, Career and Financial Readiness: money, work, enterprise and community impact

The situation: Two students, Ife and Kunle, finish school with the same grades. Ife has practised calming her nerves before presentations, asking for help early and bouncing back after a rejected scholarship form. Kunle has never had the chance to practise any of that.

How it often goes wrong: Six months into university, Kunle freezes in his first group presentation and hides a failing grade for weeks. Ife rehearses, asks her lecturer for feedback and improves. The grades matched; the toolkits did not.

b: Name the skill gap honestly, without shame
Pick one pillar and practise it weekly
Ask for feedback early, before the stakes are high

p: Mistake: waiting until you feel ready. Fix: Start small this week; readiness is built by doing, not by waiting.
Mistake: treating soft skills as extras. Fix: Treat them as core subjects that need practice, not just reading.
Mistake: comparing your Week 1 to someone else's Week 50. Fix: Measure progress against your own starting line.
(5 min) Draw six boxes, one per pillar, and give each a score from 1 to 5
(5 min) Circle your strongest pillar and star the one you most want to grow
(10 min) In pairs, tell your partner the one thing you are 'waiting to feel ready for'; your partner asks, 'What is the smallest step you could take this month?'
(10 min) Start your Letter to Future Me: who do you want to be by Week 50, and why does it matter?
Which pillar scored lowest, and what story am I telling myself about it?
What would I try this year if I knew I could not embarrass myself?
What does 'ready enough' look like for my first step?
• Future-ready is a toolkit, not a prediction
• Six pillars give the year its shape
• Starting before you feel ready is itself the skill
Self-rating (1 to 5): How confident do I feel using this skill right now, and what is one thing that would raise my score by a point?

units.title: Week 2: Growth Mindset
units.summary: Tell a fixed mindset from a growth mindset and practise reframing setbacks as useful feedback.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Spot fixed-mindset thoughts in your own self-talk
• Reframe a setback using the three-step Notice, Name, Reframe method
• Use the word 'yet' and a next step to turn 'I can't' into a plan
Draw or describe your worst-ever first attempt at something you're now good at.

sections.h: True story: Kavinayan (12 years old) (Selangor, Malaysia)
p: Kavinayan stared at the screen during his online school session, and his face completely fell. His teacher had just announced a digital art contest for the whole school. Kavinayan loved drawing with pencils, but he had absolutely no idea how to use a digital tablet or art software. His first attempt on the tablet looked like a giant, messy blob of paint, and he accidentally deleted his entire project twice. He felt like throwing the tablet out the window.

Instead of quitting, Kavinayan decided to look at his messy blob and laugh. He told himself that his brain was just stretching to learn something new. He spent the next three weeks watching free internet videos, learning how to use the digital brushes, and practicing every single afternoon. Every time he made a mistake, he just smiled and hit the "undo" button.

When the day of the contest arrived, Kavinayan submitted a beautiful digital painting of a futuristic city. He did not win the first-place trophy, but he received a special award for the most creative design. He realized that talent is not something you are just born with. With a lot of practice and a willingness to laugh at your own mistakes, you can train your brain to learn absolutely anything.
Describe a time you wanted to quit something. What happened?
What is the difference between 'I'm bad at this' and 'I'm not good at this yet'?
How did laughing at her mistakes help Kavinayan keep going?

A mindset is a set of beliefs about ability. With a fixed mindset, you believe talent is something you either have or do not. With a growth mindset, you believe abilities grow with effort, good strategies and feedback. The brain physically changes with practice, which is why the second belief is the more accurate one.

Mindset matters because it decides what you do after a setback. If a poor mark means 'I am bad at this', you avoid the subject. If it means 'my method is not working yet', you change the method. Researchers such as Carol Dweck found that how students explain failure shapes whether they try again.

b: Growth mindset: ability is built through effort, strategy and feedback, so a setback is information, not a verdict.

p: 1. Notice: catch the thought as it happens, such as 'I am just not a maths person'
2. Name: label it out loud, 'That is my fixed-mindset voice talking'
3. Reframe: rewrite it using 'yet' and a strategy: 'I have not got this yet. What have I not tried?'
4. Act: pick one small action within 24 hours, such as asking a teacher or trying a new revision method
The situation: Chinedu scores 38% in his first Chemistry test. His friend laughs and says, 'Chemistry is not for everyone.' Chinedu goes quiet and decides to stop raising his hand.
How it often goes wrong: He tells himself, 'I am not clever enough for science,' avoids the next test revision and scores lower. The belief became a self-fulfilling prophecy.

b: Notice the thought: 'I am not clever enough for science'
Name it: fixed mindset, and ask, 'What did the test actually show me?'
Reframe: 'I do not understand moles yet. I will ask Mrs Bello for one worked example and redo the questions I missed.'

p: Mistake: praising only talent ('You are so smart'). Fix: Praise strategy and effort ('That method really worked').
Mistake: faking a 'growth' smile while feeling stuck. Fix: Admit the frustration, then choose a strategy.
Mistake: thinking growth mindset means 'just try harder'. Fix: Effort needs a better strategy and feedback, not only more hours.
(5 min) List three things you say to yourself when something is hard
(5 min) Mark each one F (fixed) or G (growth)
(10 min) Rewrite every F thought using 'yet' plus a strategy
(10 min) Swap with a partner and test each other's rewrites: is there a clear next action?
Where do I give up fastest, and what thought comes just before?
Who in my life models a growth mindset, and what do they do differently?
What is one skill I believe I 'cannot' do that I could try for 20 minutes this week?
• Abilities grow with practice, strategy and feedback
• A setback is data about your method, not about your worth
• 'Not yet' plus one next action beats 'I can't'
Self-rating (1 to 5): How confident do I feel using this skill right now, and what is one thing that would raise my score by a point?

units.title: Week 3: Knowing Yourself
units.summary: Discover your strengths, interests and values and use them to choose a direction.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Identify three personal strengths with real evidence from your life
• Name two values and one cause that matter to you
• Combine strengths, interests and purpose into one 'sweet spot' statement
Name three words other people would use to describe you — then three words you'd use for yourself.

sections.h: True story: Marley Dias (11 years old) (New Jersey, USA)
p: Marley Dias loved to read books, but one afternoon she realized something that made her very frustrated. As she looked at her massive pile of school library books, she noticed that none of the characters looked like her or shared her background. All the stories were about white boys and their dogs. Marley went to her mother to complain about how annoying this was.

Her mother looked at her and asked a very important question: "What are you going to do about it?" Marley had to take a good look at herself to figure out what she truly cared about. She realized that she was a natural organizer, a loud talker, and someone who valued fairness deeply. Instead of trying to blend in or stay quiet, she decided to use her unique personality traits to make a real change.

Marley started a public drive called #1000BlackGirlBooks to find and collect stories where black girls were the main characters. Her funny, energetic videos online went viral, and she soon collected over 10,000 books for schools around the world. By taking the time to understand her own identity and strengths, Marley found her true voice and helped thousands of other kids do exactly the same.
What is something in the world around you that frustrates you the way the book pile frustrated Marley?
What are three strengths people say you have?
What would you start if you knew it could not fail?

Self-knowledge is the starting point for good choices. Your strengths are things you do well, often with energy. Your interests are what pull your attention. Your values are what you refuse to compromise on. Knowing all three helps you choose subjects, friends, projects and eventually careers that fit you.

Most people can name their weaknesses in seconds but struggle to name their strengths, because strengths feel 'normal' to the person who has them. That is why evidence and other people's observations are so useful: they show you what you cannot easily see yourself.

b: Strengths + interests + purpose = a direction worth following.

p: 1. Skill: list things you do well that others notice, with proof such as results, praise or projects
2. Spark: list activities where time disappears because you are absorbed
3. Purpose: list problems or causes you care about solving
4. Overlap: look for the point where two or three meet, and write it as one sentence: 'I am good at X, I enjoy Y, and I care about Z.'

The situation: Zainab is 14 and unsure what to do with her life. She loves organising her class WhatsApp group, is the person friends call when plans fall apart, and gets upset when younger pupils are ignored in the school yard.
How it often goes wrong: Because she is not top of Mathematics, Zainab decides she is 'not good at anything' and copies her friend's plan to study medicine.

b: Skill: organising people and calming conflicts
Spark: planning events and bringing people together
Purpose: making sure everyone is included
Overlap: 'I am good at organising, I enjoy bringing people together and I care about inclusion.' Possible paths: event management, teaching, community work, HR or law.

p: Mistake: choosing a path only because friends or parents did. Fix: Test their idea against your own triangle before you decide.
Mistake: listing only school subjects as strengths. Fix: Include character strengths such as patience, humour and fairness.
Mistake: treating the result as permanent. Fix: Retake the triangle each year; you will keep changing.
(5 min) Write five things you do well and one piece of proof for each
(5 min) Ask a neighbour: 'What do you see me doing well?' Add their answers
(10 min) Complete the three circles: Skill, Spark, Purpose
(5 min) Write your overlap sentence and read it to a partner
Which strength surprised me most when someone else named it?
When did I last lose track of time, and what was I doing?
What problem in my community bothers me enough to want to fix it?
• Strengths need evidence, not just opinions
• Interests show where your energy goes
• Purpose points your strengths toward something that matters

units.title: Week 4: Building Confidence
units.summary: Build real confidence by taking small, repeated actions instead of waiting for fear to disappear.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Explain why confidence follows action instead of coming before it
• Build a personal Courage Ladder with five rungs, from easy to hard
• Use a self-talk script and a calm-down routine before a challenge
What is something you were once terrified of that no longer scares you? What changed?

sections.h: True story: Diana Zuleta (13 years old) (Panama City, Panama)
p: Diana Zuleta was terrified of speaking in public. Whenever her teacher called on her to read a paragraph out loud in class, Diana’s heart would beat like a bass drum. Her hands would shake so much that she would drop her papers, causing her classmates to giggle. She felt like she was the least confident person on the planet.

One day, her school announced a mandatory speech competition for all students. Diana wanted to hide in the bathroom. But her older brother gave her a funny piece of advice: "Just practice your speech in front of our pet dog, Max. He won't judge your accent!" Diana actually tried it. She stood in her living room, wearing a silly hat to make herself laugh, and gave her speech to the dog, who just wagged his tail.

Every day, Diana practiced standing tall and speaking clearly. On the day of the competition, she walked up to the microphone. Her knees felt like jelly, but she remembered her practice sessions with Max. She took a deep breath, smiled at the crowd, and delivered her speech perfectly. She did not win the top prize, but as she walked off the stage, she realized the shaking had stopped. She learned that confidence is not a magical power you are born with; it is like a muscle that grows every time you face your fears.
What is something that makes your 'heart beat like a bass drum' the way public speaking did for Diana?
What is one small, brave thing you could do this week?
How is confidence different from not being scared at all?

Confidence is not the absence of fear; it is the belief that you can handle a challenge, built from evidence. Psychologists call this self-efficacy. The strongest source of it is mastery experiences: every time you do something slightly scary and survive, your brain records proof.

This means waiting to feel confident before you act is backwards. The order is act, collect proof, feel more confident, act again. Avoidance feels safe today, but it quietly makes the fear bigger tomorrow.

b: Confidence is built by small brave actions repeated over time, not by waiting for fear to disappear.

p: 1. Pick the big challenge, such as speaking in front of the class
2. List five steps toward it, ranked from easiest to hardest (for example: say your name in a small group, ask a question, give a one-minute talk to friends, speak to the class)
3. Climb one rung at a time; repeat a rung until it feels manageable before moving on
4. Collect proof: after each rung, write what happened, what you did well and what you learned
The situation: Folake wants to join the school debate club but her hands shake when she speaks in class. She tells herself she will join 'when I am not scared any more.'
How it often goes wrong: A year passes. She has not joined, the fear is the same and she now thinks, 'I am just a shy person who cannot speak.'

b: Rung 1: greet two new people this week
Rung 2: ask one question in class
Rung 3: read a 30-second opinion to a friend
Rung 4: give a one-minute talk to the debate club as a visitor
Rung 5: join a debate round as second speaker. Each success becomes proof for the next.

p: Mistake: jumping to the top rung. Fix: Choose steps that stretch you, not terrify you.
Mistake: ignoring small wins. Fix: Write them down; your brain forgets proof quickly.
Mistake: harsh self-talk ('Do not be stupid'). Fix: Talk to yourself as you would to a friend: 'This is hard, and I can do it badly the first time.'
(5 min) Write one situation where you want more confidence
(10 min) Build a five-rung Courage Ladder for it
(5 min) Write a two-sentence self-talk script, such as 'I am nervous because this matters. I will do my first step now.'
(5 min) Practise a calm-down breath: in for 4 counts, hold 4, out for 6, three times
What do I avoid, and what does avoiding it cost me?
What is the smallest rung I could climb this week?
What proof do I already have that I can do hard things?
• Action comes first, confidence follows
• Small, repeated steps beat one giant leap
• Written proof keeps your progress visible
Self-rating (1 to 5): How confident do I feel using this skill right now, and what is one thing that would raise my score by a point?

units.title: Week 5: Personal Values & Character
units.summary: Clarify your values and learn how character is shown by what you do when it is hard or nobody is watching.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Choose five personal values and define each in your own words
• Test a value against a real dilemma using the Choose, Define, Test, Act method
• Explain the difference between a value you say and a value you live
Complete the sentence — 'I could never respect someone who...' What value does that reveal?

sections.h: True story: Nihal Raj (7 years old, known as "Kicha") (Kochi, Kerala, India)
p: Nihal Raj loved cooking more than anything else. He spent hours in the kitchen with his mother, learning how to mix ingredients and bake delicious treats. He even started his own online cooking video channel, where his funny jokes and bright smile made him a hit with viewers worldwide. Soon, a major American television show noticed his talent and invited him to fly to Hollywood to cook live on TV.

A massive company saw his video and offered to pay him thousands of dollars to use his recipes to sell unhealthy junk food to kids. Nihal and his parents sat down to talk about the offer. It was a huge amount of money for a young boy. But Nihal valued health and honesty. He knew that selling bad food to his young fans was wrong, even if it made him rich.

Nihal looked at the big check and politely said no. Instead, he chose to partner with companies that made healthy snacks for children. He even donated a portion of his video earnings to local charities that fed hungry kids in his hometown. By standing firm on his personal values, Nihal proved that good character and staying true to what is right is worth much more than a pile of money.
Name three values you refuse to compromise on.
When has doing the right thing been the harder choice for you?
How do your values show up in ordinary, everyday decisions?

Values are the principles you use to decide what is right: honesty, loyalty, kindness, hard work, faith, fairness. Character is how those values show up in behaviour, especially under pressure. Anyone can say they value honesty when it costs nothing; character is tested when telling the truth is uncomfortable.

Clear values act like a compass. When friends push you to copy in an exam, to join in teasing or to take a shortcut, a decision you made in advance is far easier to follow than one you try to invent in the moment.

b: Values are your compass; character is what you actually do when the pressure is on.

sections.h: The method: The Values Compass: Choose, Define, Test, Act
p: 1. Choose: pick the five values you most want to be known for from a list of 20 or more
2. Define: write what each value looks like in action, for example 'Honesty means I tell the truth even when I will be in trouble'
3. Test: imagine a hard situation where the value costs you something and decide what you would do
4. Act: choose one value to practise visibly this week and tell someone to hold you to it
The situation: During a Mathematics test, Emeka sees that the answers are exposed on his classmate's paper. The classmate whispers, 'Copy, no one will know.'
How it often goes wrong: With no clear definition of honesty, Emeka thinks, 'Everyone does it,' copies two answers and feels sick for days. A decision made in panic became a habit.

b: He had already defined honesty as 'doing my own work even when I could get away with copying'
He tested the idea beforehand and knew the cost: a lower mark
He acts: he covers his paper, whispers 'No', and later tells the classmate he will help him revise. The value had been decided before the pressure arrived.

p: Mistake: choosing values that only sound impressive. Fix: Pick values you would defend even if no one clapped.
Mistake: having ten values. Fix: Five clear values are easier to remember and use.
Mistake: judging character by what you say. Fix: Judge it by what you do when it costs you.
(5 min) Circle ten values from the list, then cross out until five remain
(10 min) Write a one-sentence definition for each of your five
(10 min) In pairs, take one dilemma card and say what each of you would do, using your values
(5 min) Write your Values Compass on a card you can keep in your bag
Which value would I find hardest to live by this week, and why?
When did I last act against one of my values, and what did I learn?
Whose character do I admire, and what do they do that shows it?
• Values guide decisions before pressure arrives
• Character is shown by behaviour, not by words
• A short list of defined values is easier to live by
Self-rating (1 to 5): How confident do I feel using this skill right now, and what is one thing that would raise my score by a point?

units.activity: This week's challenge: Carry your Values Compass card for a week. Each night, note one moment when a value helped you decide something, and one moment when it was hard to follow. Bring your notes and your card to the next session.

check.q: Which statement best describes character?
o: How you behave when a value is tested, especially when it costs you
What you say your values are

check.q: Why is it helpful to decide your values in advance?
o: Pressure makes it hard to think, and a prior decision is easier to follow

check.q: Which is the clearest definition of honesty?
o: Telling the truth and doing my own work even when I could get away with not doing so

units.title: Week 6: Goal Setting
units.summary: Turn wishes into SMART goals with a clear plan, and prepare for obstacles with a WOOP plan.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Write one goal that is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound
• Break a goal into weekly actions and a first step you can do in 24 hours
• Use WOOP (Wish, Outcome, Obstacle, Plan) to prepare for the thing most likely to stop you
What's a goal you achieved that felt impossible when you first set it?

sections.h: True story: Yassine El Idrissi (15 years old) (Casablanca, Morocco)
p: Yassine El Idrissi had a huge dream: he wanted to build his very own working robot before he graduated high school. When he told his friends, they laughed and said he was dreaming too big because robot parts were expensive and complicated. Yassine felt discouraged, but he decided to break his massive dream down into much smaller, bite-sized goals.

He wrote a checklist in his notebook. His goal for the first month was simply to save enough pocket money to buy a single small motor. His goal for the second month was to learn how to wire that motor to a battery. He treated each small step like a level in a video game, celebrating with a little dance in his room whenever a wire finally worked.

It took Yassine fourteen months of slow, steady work. There were days when things broke, but because his daily goals were so small, he never felt completely overwhelmed. By December 2019, Yassine placed his creation on his desk, flipped the switch, and watched his small robot roll across the floor. He learned that no dream is too big if you have the patience to break it down into tiny, daily steps.
What is one goal you have never told anyone about?
What is the very first, smallest step toward that goal?
Who could help hold you accountable this year?

A wish like 'I want to do better in school' is a direction, not a goal. A goal tells you exactly what success looks like and by when. Clear goals focus attention, make progress visible and give you something to celebrate.

Goals fail less from lack of ambition than from lack of a plan for obstacles. Research by psychologist Gabriele Oettingen shows that picturing a good outcome and then planning for the main obstacle ('If this happens, then I will do that') works better than positive thinking alone.

b: A goal is a wish with a number, a date and a plan for the obstacle.

p: 1. Specific: say exactly what you will do, such as 'Raise my English score from 55% to 70%'
2. Measurable and Time-bound: decide how you will track it and the date you will check, such as 'by the end-of-term test on 12 December'
3. Achievable and Relevant: stretch, but make it possible, and link it to something you truly care about
4. WOOP: Wish, Outcome (how it will feel), Obstacle (what usually stops you), Plan ('If I feel like scrolling at 7 pm, then I will put my phone in another room and start for 20 minutes')
The situation: Bisi says, 'This year I want to be good at coding.' By March she has opened a tutorial twice.
How it often goes wrong: The goal has no number, no date and no plan for her main obstacle, which is being tired after school.

b: Specific: 'Build a simple personal website with three pages'
Measurable and time-bound: 'Complete by 30 June; finish one lesson every Tuesday and Thursday'
Obstacle plan: 'If I am too tired after school, then I will do a 15-minute lesson before dinner instead of skipping'
First step in 24 hours: create the project folder and watch lesson one.

p: Mistake: setting too many goals at once. Fix: Choose one to three priority goals.
Mistake: making a goal about outcomes you do not control, like 'be top of the class'. Fix: Add behaviour goals you control, like 'revise 30 minutes daily'.
Mistake: never reviewing. Fix: Put a weekly 10-minute review in your calendar.
(5 min) Write one wish for this term
(10 min) Turn it into a SMART goal and read it aloud to a partner
(5 min) Break it into three weekly actions and a first 24-hour step
(5 min) Complete a WOOP card with one real obstacle and an If-Then plan
Which goal from the past have I abandoned, and what really stopped me?
What does success on this goal feel like in my body and mind?
Who can I ask to check on me every week?
• SMART turns a wish into a target
• Weekly actions make big goals manageable
• If-Then planning beats hoping the obstacle will not appear
Self-rating (1 to 5): How confident do I feel using this skill right now, and what is one thing that would raise my score by a point?

units.activity: This week's challenge: Write your 1-year, 5-year and 10-year goals, then turn the 1-year goal into a full SMART goal with a WOOP plan. Start your Goal Tracker and add it to your portfolio; you will use it in the Quarter 1 Capstone.

check.q: Which is the best SMART goal?
o: Get 70% in my next maths test on 12 December by practising 30 minutes a day
Be the best in the class

check.q: What does the 'O' for Obstacle in WOOP help you do?
o: Plan ahead for the thing most likely to stop you

check.q: Femi's goal is 'be top of the class.' Which extra goal would give him more control?
o: Revise for 30 minutes every school day

units.title: Week 7: Time Management
units.summary: Take control of your hours with priorities, time-blocking and planned rest.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Sort tasks by urgency and importance using the Eisenhower matrix
• Build a one-week time-block schedule that includes study, practice and rest
• Say a polite 'no' to protect your focus
If you had one extra hour every day, what would you actually do with it?

sections.h: True story: Chloe Soh (14 years old) (Singapore)
p: Chloe Soh was a busy teenager. She played competitive badminton, took weekly piano lessons, and had a mountain of school homework every night. She was so stressed out that she kept forgetting her assignments, showing up late to sports practice, and staying up until midnight trying to finish her essays. Her life felt like a chaotic storm.

One evening, Chloe accidentally wore two different colored socks to badminton practice because she was in such a rush. Her teammates laughed, and Chloe realized she needed a better system. She decided to sit down and create a simple weekly time chart using bright, colorful markers. She blocked out exact times for studying, practicing piano, and playing sports, but she also made sure to schedule an hour just for relaxing and watching TV.

Chloe stuck the colorful chart right on her bedroom door. Whenever her friends asked her to hang out, she checked her chart first to see if she had free time. Within two weeks, Chloe stopped rushing. She was getting better grades, sleeping early, and she never wore mismatched socks to practice again. She learned that managing your time does not take away your freedom; it actually gives you your free time back.
What usually eats up your time without you noticing?
What is one task you keep postponing, and why?
How could a weekly plan change your Saturdays?

Almost nobody runs out of hours; what runs out is deliberate decisions about how those hours are used. 'I don't have time' often means 'I have not decided this matters more than what currently fills my time'. That sentence puts the choice back in your hands.

Time management is really priority management. A to-do list shows what you want to do; a calendar shows what you will do. Putting tasks into real time blocks forces honesty about how long things take and where they fit, and planned rest keeps you from burning out.

b: Decide your priorities on purpose, give them a time block, and schedule rest as part of the plan.

p: 1. Prioritise: sort tasks into four boxes: Urgent and Important (do now), Important not Urgent (schedule), Urgent not Important (delegate or shorten), Neither (drop)
2. Block: put the important tasks on a calendar with a start and end time, for example 'Homework 4:00 to 5:00 pm, phone in another room'
3. Protect: say no kindly to things that steal your blocks: 'I cannot join now, I am studying until 5. Can we meet after?'
4. Review: spend 15 minutes every Sunday evening adjusting next week's blocks based on what really happened
The situation: Temi has football on Tuesdays and Thursdays, tutorials on Wednesdays, a big Biology test in nine days and a group project due Friday. Her evenings disappear into WhatsApp and TikTok.
How it often goes wrong: She writes an enormous to-do list, panics on Thursday night, copies part of the project from a friend and studies for Biology at midnight.

b: Sort: Biology test and project are Important (and soon Urgent); TikTok is Neither
Block: Mon, Wed, Fri 5 to 6 pm Biology; Tue and Thu 7 to 7:45 pm project; Saturday morning rest and sport
Protect: tell friends, 'I am offline from 5 to 6, message me after'
Review: on Sunday, move any missed block to the next day instead of dropping it

p: Mistake: planning every minute with no slack. Fix: Leave 20 per cent of your day flexible for surprises.
Mistake: leaving rest out. Fix: Schedule sleep, meals and play as real blocks.
Mistake: starting with the hardest task at your lowest-energy time. Fix: Do demanding work in your best focus hours.
(5 min) List everything on your plate this week
(10 min) Sort it into the Eisenhower matrix
(10 min) Build a one-week time-block schedule on paper or a phone calendar
(5 min) Practise saying 'no' to a partner using the 'I cannot now, but I can later' form
What eats my time without my noticing?
Which important-but-not-urgent task do I keep postponing?
What would I do with one extra protected hour a day?
• Priorities come before schedules
• A calendar is more honest than a to-do list
• Rest belongs inside the plan
Self-rating (1 to 5): How confident do I feel using this skill right now, and what is one thing that would raise my score by a point?

units.activity: This week's challenge: Build a one-week time-block schedule and follow it for seven days. On Sunday, note which blocks worked and which did not, and adjust. Add the first and the adjusted schedules to your portfolio.

check.q: In the Eisenhower matrix, where do 'important but not urgent' tasks belong?
o: Do them immediately in a panic

check.q: Why is time-blocking often better than a long to-do list?
o: It forces you to fit tasks into real time and be honest about how long they take
It removes the need to rest

check.q: Your friends invite you out during your study block. What is the best response?
o: Say yes and study later at midnight
Say, 'I am studying until 5, can we meet after?'

units.title: Week 8: Emotional Intelligence I (Self-Awareness)
units.summary: Notice, name and manage your own emotions before they manage you.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Name at least ten different emotions beyond 'happy', 'sad' and 'angry'
• Use Pause, Label, Choose when an emotion is strong
• Tell the difference between an emotion and the action you choose
On a scale of 1–5, how easy is it for you to name what you're feeling in the moment? Why?

sections.h: True story: Juanito "Aries" Toledo (13 years old) (Cebu City, Philippines)
p: Juanito Toledo was usually a very happy student, but exam week always turned him into a completely different person. Whenever he sat down to take a math test, his throat would tighten, his palms would sweat, and he would snap angrily at anyone who tried to talk to him. He did not understand why a simple piece of paper made him feel so furious inside.

During one stressful test, Juanito dropped his eraser, and when his friend picked it up for him, Juanito yelled, "Leave me alone!" The teacher had to step in, and Juanito felt deeply embarrassed. He realized he needed to understand what was happening inside his own body. He began to notice that the anger always started with a heavy feeling in his stomach right before the test papers were handed out.

The next time he felt that heavy stomach feeling, Juanito did not ignore it. He stopped, closed his eyes, and whispered to himself: "I am not angry at my friends; I am just scared of failing this test." Simply naming the true feeling made the heavy weight in his stomach disappear. By learning to recognize his own emotions early, Juanito was able to stay calm, apologize to his friend, and pass his math test with a clear mind.
What emotion is hardest for you to name in the moment?
What usually triggers a strong reaction in you?
What helps you calm down when you feel overwhelmed?

Emotional intelligence is the ability to notice your own emotions, understand what causes them and choose how to respond. Self-awareness is its foundation: you cannot manage what you cannot name. Emotions are not good or bad; they are signals, like a dashboard light, telling you something needs attention.

When a feeling is strong, the thinking part of the brain gets harder to reach. Research on 'affect labelling' suggests that simply putting a precise word to a feeling can reduce its intensity. 'I feel disrespected' gives you something to work with in a way that 'I am just angry' does not.

b: Name it to tame it: a precise word for the feeling gives you room to choose your response.

p: 1. Pause: stop for one slow breath before you speak or act; notice where you feel it in your body
2. Label: name the feeling precisely, such as 'embarrassed', 'jealous' or 'overwhelmed', using an emotion wheel if needed
3. Choose: ask, 'What do I need right now, and what is the most helpful thing I can do?' Options include walking away, asking for help or speaking calmly
4. Review: later, ask what the feeling was trying to tell you
The situation: Dayo's team loses a football match because of a teammate's mistake. In the changing room, someone laughs. Dayo feels hot in the face and clenches his fists.
How it often goes wrong: Without pausing, he shouts at the teammate, throws his bag and is dropped from the next game. His emotion made the decision.

b: Pause: one deep breath; notice the heat in the face
Label: 'I am embarrassed and disappointed, and I feel disrespected by the laughing'
Choose: step outside for two minutes, then say calmly, 'I was upset about the loss. Let us work on that pass in training.'

p: Mistake: believing you should never feel anger or fear. Fix: All emotions are information; manage the action, not the feeling.
Mistake: using one word like 'fine' for everything. Fix: Build a wider emotion vocabulary.
Mistake: acting first, thinking later. Fix: Make the one-breath pause a habit.
(5 min) Look at an emotion wheel and write ten feelings you have had this month
(10 min) Recall a recent strong emotion and write the situation, body signals, label and what you did
(10 min) Role-play a heated moment in pairs, practising Pause, Label, Choose out loud
(5 min) Agree a private signal that reminds you to pause
Where in my body do I feel anger, fear and excitement?
Which emotion do I find hardest to admit, and why?
How would my last argument have changed with a ten-second pause?
• Emotions are signals, not commands
• A precise word reduces a feeling's power
• The gap between feeling and action is where you choose
Self-rating (1 to 5): How confident do I feel using this skill right now, and what is one thing that would raise my score by a point?

units.activity: This week's challenge: Keep a three-day Emotion Log: each evening, write the strongest feeling of the day, its trigger, its precise name and what you did. Circle one moment when you could have paused. Add the log to your portfolio.

check.q: What is the main benefit of labelling an emotion precisely?
o: It lets others guess your thoughts
It helps you understand it and choose a response

check.q: In Pause, Label, Choose, what comes first?
Which statement shows emotional self-awareness?
o: I feel embarrassed and I need a minute before I answer
I will never feel this way again
You made me angry, so I shouted

units.title: Week 9: Emotional Intelligence II (Empathy & Relationships)
units.summary: Understand other people's feelings and build stronger relationships through empathy.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Tell cognitive empathy from sympathy and explain why empathy is a skill you can practise
• Use See, Ask, Reflect Back to understand a friend's feelings
• Offer support in a way the other person actually wants
Describe a time someone's kindness changed your day, even in a small way.

sections.h: True story: Thabo Ndlovu (15 years old) (Johannesburg, South Africa)
p: Thabo Ndlovu was the most popular guy in his class, and he loved to crack jokes to make his classmates laugh. One morning, a new student named David joined the class. David wore thick glasses, sat completely quietly in the back row, and spoke with a different accent. Thabo thought it would be funny to mimic David's voice during lunchtime, and all the other kids laughed along.

But as Thabo watched David walk away alone with his head down, he saw how tightly David was clutching his backpack. Thabo suddenly remembered how terrified he had felt when he changed schools two years before. He realized his jokes were not actually funny; they were just mean.

The next day, Thabo decided to use his social skills differently. He walked over to the back row and sat right next to David during lunch. He handed David an apple, smiled, and asked him how his first week was going. The other kids saw Thabo doing this and decided to come over to join them too. Thabo learned that true emotional intelligence is not about making people laugh at someone else; it is about putting yourself in another person's shoes and using your influence to lift them up.
When did someone's empathy really help you?
How can you tell when a friend is struggling, even if they don't say it?
What is one way you can check in on someone this week?

Empathy is understanding what another person feels and why, from their point of view. It is different from sympathy, which is feeling sorry for someone from the outside, and different from agreeing, which you can do without understanding. Empathy is a skill: we get better at it by paying attention, asking and checking.

Strong relationships are built on feeling understood. Teams, friendships and families all work better when people feel their feelings are taken seriously. The good news is that empathy does not need long speeches; one accurate sentence like 'It sounds like you felt left out' can change a conversation.

b: Empathy: see the situation through the other person's eyes, check you have understood, and then help in the way they want.

sections.h: The method: See, Ask, Reflect Back
p: 1. See: notice the face, voice, body language and what changed in their behaviour
2. Ask: use open questions such as 'How are you feeling about this?' or 'What is the hardest part?'
3. Reflect back: say what you heard in your own words, 'It sounds like you are disappointed because you worked hard on this'
4. Offer: ask what would help, 'Do you want advice, or do you just want me to listen?'
The situation: Ngozi has been quiet for two days. When her friend Hauwa asks what is wrong, she says, 'Nothing, I am fine.' Her best friend did not invite her to a birthday party.
How it often goes wrong: Hauwa says, 'Do not be silly, it is only a party,' and moves on. Ngozi feels even more alone and stops talking.

b: See: Hauwa notices Ngozi eating alone and avoiding eye contact
Ask: 'You seem quiet lately. I am here if you want to talk about anything.'
Reflect back: 'It sounds like being left out really hurt.'
Offer: 'Do you want me to sit with you, or would you like ideas for what to do next?'

p: Mistake: rushing to fix or give advice. Fix: Listen first and ask if advice is wanted.
Mistake: comparing ('That is nothing, I once...'). Fix: Keep the focus on their experience.
Mistake: assuming you know how they feel. Fix: Check by asking and reflecting back.
(5 min) Read three short scenarios and write what each person might be feeling
(10 min) In pairs, one person shares a mild frustration while the other uses See, Ask, Reflect Back
(5 min) Swap roles
(5 min) Discuss: what did the reflection feel like to receive?
When did someone understand me really well, and what did they do?
Who in my life needs me to listen better right now?
Do I tend to fix, compare or listen, and what could I try instead?
• Empathy is a practised skill, not a personality type
• Reflecting back shows you are listening
• Ask what help is wanted before offering it
Self-rating (1 to 5): How confident do I feel using this skill right now, and what is one thing that would raise my score by a point?

units.activity: This week's challenge: Choose one person and have a five-minute conversation using See, Ask, Reflect Back, with no advice unless asked. Afterwards write what you learned about them and about yourself, and add it to your portfolio.

check.q: What is empathy?
o: Understanding how someone feels from their point of view

check.q: Which is a good reflecting-back sentence?
o: At least it is not a big problem
I felt worse than that once
It sounds like you felt left out, and that hurt

check.q: Before offering advice to a friend who is upset, the best step is to:
o: Ask whether they want advice or just someone to listen

units.title: Week 10: Building Positive Habits
units.summary: Design small daily habits that stick using cues, routines, rewards and 'tiny starts'.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Explain the cue, routine, reward loop behind any habit
• Design one tiny habit and attach it to something you already do
• Plan for a missed day so one slip does not become a spiral
What's one small habit you already have that you're proud of?

sections.h: True story: Lewis Pugh (13 years old) (Bristol, United Kingdom)
p: Lewis Pugh wanted to get into the best shape of his life so he could make the school football team. On New Year's Day, he came up with a massive plan: he was going to do 100 push-ups, run five miles, and eat only vegetables every single day. On day one, he did great. But by day three, his entire body was so sore that he could barely lift his arms, and he quit his new routine completely to eat chocolate on the couch.

Lewis realized his giant plan was a mistake. He decided to try a completely different approach called the "Tiny Habit Strategy." Instead of doing 100 push-ups, his new daily goal was to do just five push-ups right after he brushed his teeth in the morning. It was so incredibly easy that he couldn't find any excuse to skip it.

He did his five push-ups every single day for a month. Soon, five push-ups felt like nothing, so he naturally increased the number to ten, and then to fifteen. By the time the football tryouts arrived in September, Lewis was doing fifty push-ups easily every morning without even thinking about it. He proved that massive changes do not come from giant, exhausting efforts, but from small, positive actions repeated every single day until they become a natural habit.
What is one small habit that could make a big difference in your life?
What usually derails your good habits?
How could you redesign your environment to make a habit easier?

A habit is a behaviour repeated so often that it becomes almost automatic. Habits follow a loop: a cue (a trigger), a routine (the action) and a reward (the benefit). A UCL study found it took people an average of 66 days for a new behaviour to become automatic, but the range was huge, from 18 to 254 days, so patience matters more than perfection.

The secret to starting is to shrink the habit until it is almost too small to fail, such as one push-up or reading one page, and to attach it to something you already do. This is called habit stacking: 'After I brush my teeth, I will read one page.' Success feels good, and that feeling helps the habit stick.

b: Make it tiny, attach it to a cue, reward yourself, and never miss twice in a row.

sections.h: The method: Cue, Routine, Reward (Tiny Start)
p: 1. Choose one tiny habit that supports a goal, such as 'write one sentence in my journal'
2. Cue: attach it to an existing habit, 'After I pour my morning tea...'
3. Routine: do the tiny version (it must take under two minutes); you may do more, but you must do the tiny one
4. Reward: celebrate straight away with a tick on a tracker, a smile, or 'Yes!'; and follow the rule 'never miss twice'
The situation: Adaeze wants to read more. She promises herself one hour every night, but after a tiring day she skips it, feels guilty and gives up after four days.
How it often goes wrong: The habit is too big, has no cue and has no reward except guilt when it fails.

b: Shrink it: read one page
Attach it: 'After I get into bed, I read one page'
Reward: tick a calendar box and enjoy the streak
Plan for slips: 'If I miss a day, I read two pages the next night, but I never skip twice.'

p: Mistake: starting with five new habits. Fix: Build one at a time.
Mistake: relying on motivation. Fix: Rely on cues and environment, like leaving your book on your pillow.
Mistake: giving up after one missed day. Fix: Use the 'never miss twice' rule.
(5 min) Choose one habit that would help a goal
(5 min) Shrink it to a two-minute version
(10 min) Write the habit stack: 'After I ____, I will ____'
(10 min) Design a simple tracker and a reward; share your plan with a partner who will check in
Which of my current habits help me most, and which hurt?
What cue could I attach my new habit to?
What do I say to myself when I miss a day?
• Habits run on cue, routine and reward
• Tiny starts beat big promises
• Never miss twice
Self-rating (1 to 5): How confident do I feel using this skill right now, and what is one thing that would raise my score by a point?

units.activity: This week's challenge: Run your tiny habit for 14 days using a tracker. At the end, write what helped, what got in the way and how you will adjust. Add the tracker to your portfolio; it feeds your Quarter 1 Capstone.

check.q: What are the three parts of the habit loop?
Why make a new habit tiny?
o: Because small habits do not matter
So it is easy to start and hard to fail

check.q: You miss your habit on Monday. What does 'never miss twice' tell you to do?
o: Do it on Tuesday, even if only the tiny version

units.title: Week 11: Resilience & Overcoming Failure
units.summary: Bounce back from failure by treating it as information, getting support and choosing a next step.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Explain resilience as a set of skills, not a trait you are born with
• Use Feel, Learn, Support, Next Step after a setback
• Write a 'failure resume' that turns setbacks into lessons
Share a time you failed at something publicly. What did you do next?

sections.h: True story: Gitanjali Rao (10 years old) (Lone Tree, Colorado, USA)
p: Gitanjali Rao was watching the news with her parents when she learned about a terrible crisis in Flint, Michigan. The city's drinking water was contaminated with dangerous chemicals, and thousands of young kids were getting sick from drinking it. Gitanjali felt a deep urge to help, so she decided to invent a cheap, fast device that could test water safety instantly.

She spent months working on her invention in her family's kitchen, using a small computer chip and various sensors. But nothing worked on the first try. Her device failed to turn on twenty times in a row, and her sensors kept giving completely incorrect readings. Gitanjali felt frustrated and wondered if she was simply too young to solve such a massive adult problem.

Instead of throwing her broken prototype in the trash, Gitanjali treated each failure like a valuable clue. She reached out to clean-water scientists online, fixed her messy wiring mistakes, and kept testing her device over and over again. After two years of constant failures and adjustments, her device, which she named Tethys, worked perfectly. At age 12, she won the title of "America’s Top Young Scientist." Gitanjali showed the world that failure is not the opposite of success; it is just a necessary step on the road to getting things right.
Gitanjali failed many prototypes before succeeding — what does that tell you about failure?
Describe a setback you experienced and what you learned from it.
What helps you get back up after disappointment?

Resilience is the ability to recover and keep growing after a setback. It is not about being tough or hiding pain; resilient people feel disappointment too. What differs is what they do next: they allow the feeling, find the lesson, lean on other people and take one small step forward.

Everyone who has achieved something has a hidden list of failures: rejected applications, lost matches, projects that flopped. Seeing failure as a normal part of learning removes much of its sting. The question shifts from 'What is wrong with me?' to 'What can this teach me?'

b: Resilience: feel it, learn from it, ask for support, then take one small next step.

sections.h: The method: Feel, Learn, Support, Next Step
p: 1. Feel: allow the disappointment for a short, set time instead of pretending it is not there
2. Learn: ask, 'What happened? What was in my control? What would I do differently?'
3. Support: tell one trusted person; talking shrinks the problem and brings ideas
4. Next step: choose one small, specific action within 24 hours, such as booking a retake or asking for feedback
The situation: Seun submits a science fair project and does not make the finals. His classmates celebrate the winners while he sits quietly, thinking, 'I wasted three months.'
How it often goes wrong: He deletes the project and refuses to enter again, so he never discovers that the judges only wanted a clearer explanation of his results.

b: Feel: take the evening to be disappointed, then stop
Learn: ask a judge for feedback; he learns his data was good but his explanation was confusing
Support: talk to his teacher and a friend who entered last year
Next step: redo the slides this week and enter the regional fair

p: Mistake: bottling feelings up. Fix: Name the emotion and tell someone you trust.
Mistake: blaming only yourself or only others. Fix: Separate what you controlled from what you did not.
Mistake: hiding failure. Fix: Share what you learned; it helps others too.
(5 min) Write one setback from the last year
(10 min) Run Feel, Learn, Support, Next Step on it in writing
(10 min) Start a 'Failure Resume': three failures, what each taught you, and what you did next
(5 min) Share one lesson with a partner
Which setback taught me the most, and how do I know?
Who do I turn to when things go wrong, and who should I add?
What is one thing I avoid because I fear failing at it?
• Failure is information, not identity
• Support makes setbacks smaller
• One small next step restarts momentum
Self-rating (1 to 5): How confident do I feel using this skill right now, and what is one thing that would raise my score by a point?

units.title: Week 13: Communication Fundamentals
units.summary: Say what you mean clearly, simply and in an order people can follow.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Describe communication as a loop between sender and receiver
• Structure any message using PREP: Point, Reason, Example, Point
• Adapt your words, tone and channel to your audience
Retell a piece of news in exactly one sentence.

sections.h: True story: Joshua Williams (17 years old) (Miami, Florida, USA)
p: Joshua Williams ran a foundation that collected food for families in need. He had a big meeting with a grocery store manager to ask for a donation of one hundred boxes of cereal. Joshua was nervous, so he wrote a long, three-page speech. During the meeting, he started reading his papers, talking very fast about global hunger facts, and using complicated business words he found online.

The manager looked confused and kept checking his watch. Joshua realized he was losing his audience. He stopped reading, took a breath, and decided to simplify his message. He laughed at himself, closed his notebook, and said, "Sir, to be simple, we have fifty hungry kids in the neighborhood next door who need breakfast this Saturday. Can you help us feed them?"

The manager’s face instantly changed. He smiled and said, "Yes, absolutely." Joshua learned that good communication is not about using big words or giving long speeches. It is about keeping your message simple, clear, and direct so the other person can easily understand how to help.
Why did Joshua's long speech fail where his simple sentence worked?
What is a time you over-explained something that should have been simple?
How would you explain your favourite hobby in one sentence to a stranger?

Communication is not what you say; it is what the other person understands. Every message travels from a sender, through a channel, to a receiver, and noise (distractions, assumptions, emotions) can distort it at every stage. The sender is responsible for checking that the meaning arrived.

Clear communicators lead with their main point, keep sentences short and support claims with a reason and an example. Whether you are asking a teacher for an extension or pitching an idea to your team, a clear structure makes you easier to say yes to.

b: Good communication is measured by what the listener understood, not by what the speaker said.

sections.h: The method: PREP: Point, Reason, Example, Point
p: 1. Point: state your main message in one sentence first, 'I would like an extension on my essay.'
2. Reason: give one clear reason, 'I was ill for three days and missed two lessons.'
3. Example: add a specific detail, 'I have a doctor's note and I have already finished the plan and first paragraph.'
4. Point: repeat the request, 'So could I please submit on Friday instead of Wednesday?'
The situation: Ibrahim needs help on a group project. In the group chat he writes a long message with a joke, a complaint about another member, a vague hint and no clear request.
How it often goes wrong: Nobody replies for a day. Each person thinks someone else will answer, and the work stalls.

b: Point: 'Can someone take the slides for Thursday?'
Reason: 'I am finishing the research and will be late'
Example: 'The slides only need the three headings we agreed, about 30 minutes of work'
Point: 'Please reply with a thumbs-up if you can take them.'

p: Mistake: burying the main point in the middle. Fix: Lead with the point.
Mistake: using jargon or long sentences. Fix: Choose short, plain words.
Mistake: never checking understanding. Fix: Ask, 'Does that make sense? What questions do you have?'
(5 min) Take a long, messy message and underline the real point
(10 min) Rewrite three messages (an email, a text and a spoken request) using PREP
(10 min) In pairs, deliver one PREP message aloud; the listener repeats back what they understood
(5 min) Compare: was the meaning the same?
When was I misunderstood recently, and what could I have said differently?
Do I adjust how I talk to teachers, friends and elders, and why?
Which of my messages are too long?
• Meaning is what the receiver understands
• Lead with your point
• Check understanding instead of assuming it

check.q: In the PREP method, what comes first?

units.title: Week 14: Active Listening
units.summary: Learn to listen fully so that people feel heard and you actually understand them.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Show the difference between hearing, listening and waiting to speak
• Practise RASA: Receive, Appreciate, Summarise, Ask
• Use paraphrasing to check you have understood
Pair up. One person talks for 60 seconds about their weekend; the other may not speak at all — only listen.

sections.h: True story: Richard Turere (21 years old) (Kitengela, Kenya)
p: Richard Turere grew up protecting his family's cows from lions. When he was younger, he invented "Lion Lights"—a system of flashing lights that kept predators away. Because of his cool invention, he was invited to help a nearby community where lions were still attacking livestock. In the first meeting, the village elders were angry and shouting. Richard wanted to interrupt them immediately to explain how smart his technology was.

Instead, Richard chose to keep his mouth shut and listen with his eyes and ears. He did not look at his phone or think about his next sentence. He noticed that the elders were not just mad about the cows; they were actually terrified for the safety of their children who walked to school in the dark.

Because Richard listened to their deeper fears, he did not just install lights around the cow pens. He also put lights along the dark school paths. The elders were amazed and thanked him warmly. Richard realized that active listening means hearing what people are feeling, not just the words they are saying.
What did Richard hear that the words alone did not say?
When was the last time you felt truly listened to?
What gets in the way of your listening fully to someone?

Hearing is a sense; listening is a skill. Most of us listen at the speed of thought, which is much faster than speech, so our minds wander, plan replies or judge. Active listening means giving full attention, showing it and checking you understood.

Being listened to is rare, so it is powerful. A friend who listens well gets trusted with more, a teacher who listens learns what students really need, and a leader who listens avoids expensive mistakes. Listening is the cheapest way to win respect.

b: Listen to understand, not to reply.

sections.h: The method: RASA: Receive, Appreciate, Summarise, Ask
p: 1. Receive: put your phone away, face the speaker, make comfortable eye contact and do not interrupt
2. Appreciate: use small signals such as nodding and 'mm-hm' so the speaker knows you are following
3. Summarise: say it back in your own words, 'So you are saying...'
4. Ask: pose an open question that digs deeper, 'What was the hardest part for you?'
The situation: Kemi tries to tell her older brother Tunde that she is worried about her exams. Tunde is scrolling on his phone and replies, 'Yeah, yeah, you will be fine,' without looking up.
How it often goes wrong: Kemi stops talking and feels that her worries are silly. Tunde never learns that she needs help with revision.

b: Receive: Tunde puts the phone face down and turns to her
Appreciate: nods as she speaks
Summarise: 'You are worried because you feel behind in Chemistry?'
Ask: 'What would help most: a revision plan, or someone to quiz you?'

p: Mistake: interrupting to share your own story. Fix: Wait until they finish, then ask a question.
Mistake: planning your reply while they speak. Fix: Focus on their words and emotion.
Mistake: multitasking. Fix: Give 100 per cent attention, even if only for five minutes.
(5 min) Listening test: a partner speaks for one minute while you do nothing but listen, then repeat the key points
(10 min) Practise RASA in trios: speaker, listener, observer who checks each step
(5 min) Rotate roles
(5 min) Discuss which signals made you feel most heard
Who listens to me best and what do they do?
What makes me stop listening: boredom, disagreement, my phone?
Whom do I need to listen to more carefully this week?
• Listening is active, not passive
• Summarising proves you understood
• Questions show you care
Self-rating (1 to 5): How confident do I feel using this skill right now, and what is one thing that would raise my score by a point?

units.activity: This week's challenge: Have two conversations this week where you use RASA fully, with your phone away. Afterwards, note what the speaker revealed that you would otherwise have missed. Add a short reflection to your portfolio.

check.q: What does 'summarise' in RASA mean?
o: Repeat the speaker's main points in your own words

check.q: Which is an open question?
o: What was the hardest part for you?

check.q: A friend is telling you a worry while you check your phone. What is the problem?
o: Your lack of full attention tells them they do not matter

units.title: Week 15: Public Speaking
units.summary: Prepare, structure and deliver short talks confidently, and manage your nerves.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Plan a 2-minute talk with an opening, three points and a close
• Use voice, pace and pause to keep an audience with you
• Manage speaking nerves with preparation and breathing
In 30 seconds, without notes, tell the group about your favourite meal.

sections.h: True story: Marinel Ubaldo (22 years old) (Tacloban, Philippines)
p: Marinel Ubaldo was invited to speak at a massive global conference about climate change. She had to stand on a stage in front of hundreds of world leaders and television cameras. As she walked up to the microphone, she felt completely terrified. Her hands were sweating, and she thought about running back to her seat.

She looked out at the audience of adults in expensive suits. She realized that if she spoke in a boring, robotic voice, they would ignore her. She smiled, took a deep breath, and stood up straight. Instead of reading from a script, she looked directly into their eyes and spoke loudly and clearly from her heart about her home village.

The crowd sat in total silence, listening to every single word. When she finished, the entire room stood up to cheer. Marinel learned that public speaking is not about being a perfect actor. It is about standing tall, speaking clearly, and having the courage to share your true message with the world.
What made Marinel's speech land with world leaders, when a 'perfect' script might not have?
What topic could you speak passionately about for two minutes, unscripted?
What is your biggest fear about public speaking, and where does it come from?

Public speaking ranks among the most common fears, yet it is a skill that improves quickly with deliberate practice. Nerves are normal: they are your body preparing for something important. Great speakers do not remove nerves; they channel them into energy and prepare so well that the nerves have less to attack.

A good talk is simple. It has a hook that wins attention, a clear message, no more than three main points and a strong ending. Audiences forget details but remember how clear, honest and alive you were.

b: Prepare, structure, practise out loud and let your nerves become energy.

sections.h: The method: Open, Three Points, Close
p: 1. Open: start with a hook such as a surprising fact, a question or a short story, then say your main message
2. Three points: give three points maximum, each with one example or a story
3. Close: summarise the three points and end with a call to action or a memorable line
4. Practise: rehearse out loud at least three times, standing up, and time yourself
The situation: Chidi has to present his science project to the class. He writes a long script, reads from his paper, speaks very fast and ends with 'That is all, thank you.'
How it often goes wrong: His classmates lose focus after 30 seconds. He forgets the key finding and feels it was a disaster.

b: Open: 'Did you know that a plastic bottle can last 450 years? My project shows a way to reuse it in three steps.'
Three points: collect, clean, reuse, each with a quick example
Close: 'Next time you finish a bottle, ask: collect, clean, reuse?'
Practise: rehearse three times, using notes with only keywords, and pause after each point.

p: Mistake: reading every word. Fix: Use keyword notes and look up.
Mistake: speaking too fast. Fix: Pause at the end of each sentence and breathe.
Mistake: apologising ('Sorry, I am not good at this'). Fix: Begin with confidence; the audience is on your side.
(5 min) Pick a topic you know and choose a hook
(10 min) Build a three-point outline on one page
(10 min) Deliver a 2-minute talk to a partner; they time you and note one strength and one improvement
(5 min) Do a second round using the feedback
What happens in my body when I speak, and what helps?
Which speaker do I admire, and what do they do well?
What topic could I talk about with real energy?
• Nerves are normal and manageable
• Structure keeps you and the audience on track
• Practice out loud beats silent revision
Self-rating (1 to 5): How confident do I feel using this skill right now, and what is one thing that would raise my score by a point?

units.activity: This week's challenge: Deliver a two-minute talk on a topic you care about to at least two different audiences (for example family and friends). Record or note feedback each time and add your outline and reflection to your portfolio.

check.q: How many main points are best for a short talk?
What is the best way to deal with speaking nerves?
o: Prepare well, practise out loud and breathe slowly

check.q: Why use keyword notes instead of a full script?
o: It is easier to forget words
Notes let you look up and sound natural

units.title: Week 16: Storytelling
units.summary: Use story structure to make your message memorable and persuasive.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Explain why stories are remembered better than facts alone
• Build a personal story using Situation, Struggle, Solution, Lesson
• Tell a 90-second story that connects to your audience
What's a story (a film, a book, a family story) that has stuck with you for years? Why that one?

sections.h: True story: Htet Myet Aung (16 years old) (Yangon, Myanmar)
p: Htet Myet Aung wanted to convince his school principal to start a plastic recycling club. He gathered a huge pile of papers filled with charts, percentages, and scientific data about plastic trash. He gave a presentation to the principal, listing fact after fact. The principal just nodded politely but said the school did not have the budget for a new club.

Htet realized that dry facts were not enough to make people care. The next day, he asked to speak to the principal again. This time, he did not bring any charts. Instead, he told a story about a stray dog that lived near the school yard that got its muzzle stuck in a plastic snack bag that morning. He described how the students had to work together to carefully cut the bag off to save the frightened animal.

The principal's eyes widened, and he looked genuinely touched. He immediately approved the recycling club. Htet learned that while data is important, a good story connects with people's emotions and inspires them to take action.
What makes a story easy to remember compared to a list of facts?
What personal story could you tell that carries a lesson for others?
How is a good story different from just a list of events?

Humans have shared stories for tens of thousands of years, and our brains are wired to remember them. A story places facts in a sequence with a character, a problem and a change, which gives the listener something to feel and picture. That is why people often forget the slides but remember the story.

Good stories are not long or fancy. A true, specific moment, such as the day you failed a test or helped a stranger, can teach more than a lecture. Stories build trust because they show who you are, not just what you know.

b: Facts tell, stories stick: give your message a character, a struggle and a change.

sections.h: The method: The Story Spine: Situation, Struggle, Solution, Lesson
p: 1. Situation: set the scene in one or two sentences, who, where, when
2. Struggle: describe the problem or challenge honestly, including how you felt
3. Solution: explain what you did or what changed, with specific details
4. Lesson: finish with what you learned and why it matters to your listener
The situation: Hassana must introduce herself at a leadership camp. She says: 'My name is Hassana, I am 14, I like reading and I want to be a leader.' Nobody remembers it.
How it often goes wrong: She lists facts without a story, so nothing sticks and she blends into the crowd.

b: Situation: 'Last year I was too shy to speak in class.'
Struggle: 'When my teacher asked me to read aloud, my voice shook and I wanted to disappear.'
Solution: 'I joined the school radio club and read the news every Friday for a term.'
Lesson: 'Now I know that courage is a muscle: I want to help other shy students find their voice.'

p: Mistake: starting with a long background. Fix: Start close to the action.
Mistake: leaving out the struggle. Fix: A story needs a problem to matter.
Mistake: ending without a lesson. Fix: Link the story to your listener's life.
(5 min) List three moments from your life that changed you
(10 min) Choose one and draft it using the Story Spine
(10 min) Tell it to a partner in 90 seconds; they note the most vivid detail
(5 min) Trim anything that does not support the lesson
Which story from my life shows who I really am?
What detail would make my story more vivid?
Whom could I tell my story to this week, and what would I want them to take away?
• Stories are easier to remember than facts
• Honesty about the struggle builds trust
• End with a lesson that connects to the listener
Self-rating (1 to 5): How confident do I feel using this skill right now, and what is one thing that would raise my score by a point?
