check.q: What does a good story need in order to matter?
Why do stories help people remember messages?
o: They link facts to emotions and images

check.q: In the Story Spine, what does 'Lesson' do?
o: Connects the story to why it matters to the listener

units.title: Week 17: Body Language
units.summary: Understand how posture, face, eyes and voice send messages before you say a word.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Describe the four channels of body language: posture, face, eyes and voice
• Match your body language to your words so people trust you
• Read others' signals carefully without jumping to conclusions
Without speaking, use only your body to show 'I'm excited' — then 'I'm bored.'

sections.h: True story: Kokona Hiraki (12 years old) (Tokyo, Japan)
p: Kokona Hiraki was the youngest skateboarder at the Tokyo Olympic Games. Before her final run, she was incredibly nervous. She noticed that some of her older competitors were standing with their arms crossed, looking down at the floor, and frowning. Their bodies looked tight and full of fear.

Kokona decided to use her body language to change her mindset. She stood up perfectly straight, put her hands on her hips like a superhero, and forced a big smile onto her face, even though she was trembling inside. She gave her coach a high-five and walked onto the skatepark with her head held high.

Her open and confident posture helped her body relax, and she pulled off an amazing performance to win the silver medal. Kokona proved that your body language does not just show others how you feel—it actually tells your own brain to be brave and confident.
What does closed-off body language communicate, even when the words are positive?
When have you 'read the room' through body language alone?
What is one body-language habit you want to change?

People form impressions in seconds, and much of it comes from non-verbal signals: how you stand, whether you smile, where you look, how you sound. When your words and your body language disagree, people usually believe the body. Saying 'I am happy to help' with crossed arms and a frown does not feel believable.

Body language is also not a secret code. A single signal can mean many things: crossed arms may mean cold, not hostile. The skill is to notice clusters of signals, stay curious and, when in doubt, ask. It is also something you can adjust, such as standing tall or pausing, to feel and look more confident.

b: Align your words with your posture, face, eyes and voice, and read others with curiosity, not certainty.

sections.h: The method: The Four Channels: Posture, Face, Eyes, Voice
p: 1. Posture: stand or sit tall with open shoulders; avoid hiding behind arms or a bag
2. Face: let your expression match your message; a natural smile at the start helps
3. Eyes: share eye contact in short, comfortable bursts; look at people one by one when presenting
4. Voice: vary volume, pace and tone; slow down and pause on key points
The situation: Obinna goes into an interview for a youth leadership programme. He mumbles, looks at the floor, slouches and says, 'I am very passionate.'
How it often goes wrong: The panel sees nervousness and hears low energy, so they doubt his claim.

b: Posture: sit upright with feet flat and hands relaxed
Face: smile when greeting and show interest while listening
Eyes: make eye contact with whoever asks the question, then glance to others
Voice: speak a little slower and clearer, and pause before answering

p: Mistake: copying a 'power pose' without meaning it. Fix: Aim to look natural, not forced.
Mistake: assuming one gesture proves what someone feels. Fix: Look for clusters and check by asking.
Mistake: staring without breaks. Fix: Use soft eye contact for a few seconds at a time.
(5 min) Say 'I am really happy to be here' with three different body languages and ask a partner what they believed
(10 min) Watch a short clip with the sound off and describe what you think is happening
(10 min) Practise a one-minute introduction using the Four Channels
(5 min) Give each other one comment on a strength and one adjustment
What does my body do when I am nervous?
Which signals do I notice most in others?
Whose body language makes me feel at ease and why?
• Body language often outweighs words
• Match your signals to your message
• Read others with curiosity and ask when unsure
Self-rating (1 to 5): How confident do I feel using this skill right now, and what is one thing that would raise my score by a point?

units.activity: This week's challenge: Practise the Four Channels in three real situations this week (for example greeting, answering a question, thanking someone). Ask a trusted person for feedback and note one thing to keep and one to change. Add your notes to your portfolio.

check.q: What do people usually believe when words and body language disagree?
Why should you be careful when reading body language?

check.q: Which set of signals best supports a message of confidence?
o: Open posture, steady voice and comfortable eye contact

units.title: Week 18: Teamwork
units.summary: Work well in a team: share roles, agree rules and handle the stages of group work.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Describe the four stages teams go through: forming, storming, norming, performing
• Agree a team charter with roles, rules and a way to decide
• Give and receive feedback that helps the team
Name a team (sports, school, family) you were proud to be part of. What made it work?

sections.h: True story: Precious, Blessing, and Favour (15-16 years old) (Lagos, Nigeria)
p: Three high school girls entered a tech competition to build a mobile app that could locate clean drinking water sources. At first, their teamwork was a complete disaster. Precious wanted to do all the coding herself, Blessing wanted to handle all the design, and Favour thought her own ideas were the only ones that made sense. They spent their first week arguing and got absolutely zero work done.

Their school mentor noticed the chaos and made them play a funny game: they had to tie their ankles together and try to walk across the room. Every time someone tried to run ahead, they all fell over laughing. They realized that a team cannot move forward if everyone is pulling in different directions.

They sat down and divided the work based on their specific strengths, promising to listen to each other's feedback without getting upset. By working together smoothly, they finished their app on time and won the regional tech prize. They learned that real teamwork means combining your different talents to achieve a goal that no one could reach alone.
What role do you naturally take on in a team — organiser, encourager, doer, ideas person?
Describe a team you were proud to be part of. What made it work?
What makes a team fall apart?

Almost every important task today, from a school project to a company launch, is done in teams. A good team is more than a group of friendly people: it has clear roles, shared goals and agreed ways of working. Psychologist Bruce Tuckman described stages most teams pass through: forming (getting to know each other), storming (friction), norming (agreeing how to work) and performing (doing great work).

Disagreement in the storming stage is normal and does not mean the team has failed. Teams that talk early about roles, communication and deadlines move through it faster. A short team charter written at the start prevents most of the arguments that wreck group projects.

b: Great teams agree on roles, rules and goals early, and treat disagreement as part of the process.

p: 1. Goal: write one sentence saying what success looks like, and the deadline
2. Roles: assign clear jobs such as lead, researcher, designer, presenter and time-keeper; everyone has one
3. Rules: agree how you will communicate (group chat, meeting days), how you decide (discuss, then vote) and what happens if someone misses a deadline
4. Check-in: schedule a short review at the halfway point to adjust roles and share feedback
The situation: A group of four students has two weeks to build a model of a water filter. Two members do all the work, one keeps joking and one never replies to messages.
How it often goes wrong: With no charter, resentment grows. The hard workers complain to the teacher and the project is submitted late and incomplete.

b: Goal: 'A working filter and a three-minute demo by Friday the 14th'
Roles: designer, builder, tester, presenter
Rules: reply to messages within 24 hours; meet Tuesday and Thursday for 30 minutes; if someone is stuck, ask early
Check-in: on day seven, review who needs help and swap tasks if needed

p: Mistake: letting one person do everything. Fix: Give each person a role and a visible task.
Mistake: avoiding conflict until it explodes. Fix: Raise issues early, using calm 'I' statements.
Mistake: judging members by personality instead of contribution. Fix: Discuss behaviour and outcomes, not character.
(5 min) In groups of four, choose a mini-project, such as planning a class event
(10 min) Write a team charter: goal, roles, rules, check-in
(10 min) Run a mock 'storming' moment: one member misses a deadline; practise resolving it respectfully
(5 min) Share one lesson with the class
What role do I naturally take in groups, and what role would stretch me?
What was my best team experience, and what made it work?
What do I do when I disagree with a teammate?
• Teams work best with shared goals and clear roles
• Storming is normal and solvable
• A charter prevents most conflict
Self-rating (1 to 5): How confident do I feel using this skill right now, and what is one thing that would raise my score by a point?

units.activity: This week's challenge: Use a team charter in a real group task this week (school, church, sport or family). Record what worked and what you would change. Add your charter and reflection to your portfolio.

check.q: Which stage of Tuckman's model usually involves friction between members?
What is the main purpose of a team charter?
o: To agree goals, roles and rules early

check.q: Two members do all the work while others coast. What would have helped most?

units.title: Week 19: Conflict Resolution
units.summary: Handle disagreements calmly, express your needs clearly and find solutions that work for both sides.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Describe conflict as a normal difference in needs, not a fight to win
• Use 'I' statements: Observe, Feel, Need, Request
• Aim for a solution that meets both sides' key needs
What's your instinctive first reaction when conflict starts — fight, avoid, or try to fix it?

sections.h: True story: Jordan and Taylor (14 years old) (Chicago, Illinois, USA)
p: Jordan and Taylor were the co-captains of their school's science fair project. Two days before the deadline, they got into a massive argument. Jordan wanted to paint their display board bright blue, while Taylor insisted it should be neon green. They started shouting at each other, calling each other stubborn, and both threatened to quit the project completely.

Their science teacher stepped in before things got worse. She told them they could not talk about colors for five minutes. Instead, they had to answer one question: "What is the goal of this board?" Both boys admitted they just wanted the judges to read their text clearly.

Jordan realized neon green was too bright to read, and Taylor realized dark blue was too boring. They calmed down, stopped attacking each other's personalities, and decided to compromise by using a clean, light grey background with neat black letters. They resolved the conflict by focusing on the actual problem instead of their anger, and their project received a perfect score.
What is your instinctive reaction when conflict starts — fight, avoid, or fix?
Describe a conflict that was resolved well. What made it work?
How can disagreement actually make a team stronger?

Conflict happens whenever people with different needs, values or goals share a space. It is not the same as fighting. Handled badly, conflict damages friendships; handled well, it clarifies expectations and can strengthen relationships.

Most conflicts escalate because we attack the person ('You are lazy') instead of describing the problem ('The dishes were left yesterday'). Psychologist Marshall Rosenberg's approach, called nonviolent communication, uses four steps: observe, feel, need, request. It keeps the conversation about needs and solutions rather than blame.

b: Describe the behaviour, own your feeling, state your need and make a clear request.

sections.h: The method: Observe, Feel, Need, Request
p: 1. Observe: describe what happened without judgement, 'You were 30 minutes late to our meeting'
2. Feel: say how you felt, 'I felt frustrated and unimportant'
3. Need: say what you need, 'I need reliable timing so our work gets done'
4. Request: ask for a specific action, 'Could you text me if you will be late?' and listen to their side
The situation: Nneka and her cousin share a bedroom. Nneka has an exam tomorrow, but her cousin keeps playing loud music.
How it often goes wrong: Nneka shouts, 'You are so selfish!' Her cousin shouts back and they do not speak for two days.

b: Observe: 'The music has been loud for an hour.'
Feel: 'I feel stressed because I am worried about my exam.'
Need: 'I need quiet to study until 9 pm.'
Request: 'Could you use headphones until 9, and I will leave you alone for the rest of the evening?'

p: Mistake: using 'always' and 'never'. Fix: Describe the specific event.
Mistake: bringing up old issues. Fix: Stick to the one problem.
Mistake: winning the argument. Fix: Aim for a solution both can live with.
(5 min) Read three conflict scenarios and rewrite blaming sentences into 'I' statements
(10 min) Role-play a real-life conflict in pairs using Observe, Feel, Need, Request
(5 min) Swap roles
(5 min) Discuss how it felt to hear an 'I' statement compared with an attack
How do I usually react in conflict: fight, flee, freeze or fix?
Which conflict from the past needs repair?
What need was hidden behind my last argument?
• Conflict is normal; harm is optional
• Observe, Feel, Need, Request keeps talks calm
• Look for solutions where both sides get what matters
Self-rating (1 to 5): How confident do I feel using this skill right now, and what is one thing that would raise my score by a point?

units.activity: This week's challenge: Use Observe, Feel, Need, Request in one real disagreement this week (or rehearse it in writing if no conflict arises). Write what happened and what you would adjust next time, and add it to your portfolio.

check.q: Which sentence is an 'I' statement?
o: I felt ignored when my idea was skipped, and I need to be heard

check.q: What is the aim of a win-win approach?
o: To find a solution that meets both sides' key needs

check.q: Why avoid words like 'always' and 'never' in conflicts?
o: They exaggerate and make the other person defensive

units.title: Week 20: Negotiation
units.summary: Negotiate by focusing on interests, preparing options and finding trades that both sides can accept.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Tell the difference between positions and interests
• Prepare for a negotiation with a goal, a walk-away point and options
• Use Ask, Offer, Trade to reach a fair agreement
What's something you successfully negotiated recently, even a small thing?

sections.h: True story: Aarav Mehta (15 years old) (Mumbai, India)
p: Aarav wanted his school to allow students to wear casual clothes on Fridays instead of their strict school uniforms. He went to the principal’s office and demanded the change, saying uniforms were boring. The principal immediately said no, explaining that uniforms keep the school looking neat and disciplined.

Aarav realized that demanding things never works in a negotiation. He had to think about what the principal cared about. He went back to his classmates and proposed a deal. He returned to the principal with a polite plan: "If we wear casual clothes on Fridays, every student will pay a small fee, and we will donate all that money to a local children's hospital. Plus, we promise no torn or inappropriate clothing."

The principal smiled. He saw that Aarav’s plan maintained school discipline while helping a great cause. He agreed to the deal. Aarav learned that negotiation is not about winning an argument; it is about finding a smart solution where both sides get something they want.
What is the difference between negotiating to 'win' and negotiating for a fair outcome?
Describe a time you negotiated for something — with a parent, teacher, or friend.
What would you need to prepare before an important negotiation?

Negotiation is not only for business deals. You negotiate whenever you ask for a later deadline, agree who does which chore or decide where to eat. The aim is a fair agreement that both sides will keep, not to defeat the other person.

The classic mistake is arguing about positions (what each person says they want) instead of interests (why they want it). Two sisters fighting over the last orange may discover that one wants the juice and the other wants the peel for a cake: both can win. Preparation matters too: know what you want, what you can give and what you will do if there is no deal.

b: Look behind positions to interests, prepare your options, then trade so both sides gain.

sections.h: The method: Prepare, Ask, Offer, Trade
p: 1. Prepare: write your goal, your minimum acceptable outcome and your best alternative if there is no deal
2. Ask: start by asking questions to understand their interests, 'What is most important to you here?'
3. Offer: share your interests and propose options; give a reason, not just a demand
4. Trade: swap things that cost you little but matter to them, such as 'If you help with the poster, I will present'; then confirm the agreement
The situation: Musa wants his parents to extend his weekend curfew from 8 pm to 10 pm. They say no, because they worry about safety. Musa sulks and slams the door.
How it often goes wrong: He argues only about the time. His parents dig in, and he loses the chance to discuss the real concern.

b: Prepare: goal 10 pm; minimum 9 pm; plan B is a trial for one month
Ask: 'What worries you most about me being out late?' They say transport and knowing where he is
Offer: 'I will share my location, travel with two friends and text when I arrive.'
Trade: 'Can we try 9:30 pm for one month, then review?' They agree.

p: Mistake: opening with an extreme demand. Fix: Be ambitious but reasonable.
Mistake: treating it as a fight. Fix: Remember you must live with the person afterwards.
Mistake: accepting the first offer. Fix: Ask for a moment to think and explore trades.
(5 min) Read a scenario with two positions and list each person's possible interests
(10 min) In pairs, negotiate a classroom or home rule using Prepare, Ask, Offer, Trade
(5 min) Swap sides and replay
(5 min) Debrief: what trades surprised you?
What do I usually negotiate for: time, money, attention, freedom?
Do I give in too fast or push too hard?
Which relationship needs a fairer agreement?
• Interests matter more than positions
• Preparation changes outcomes
• The best deals create value for both sides
Self-rating (1 to 5): How confident do I feel using this skill right now, and what is one thing that would raise my score by a point?

units.activity: This week's challenge: Plan and conduct one real negotiation this week (for example chores, screen time, a deadline). Write your preparation, the outcome and what you would change. Add it to your portfolio.

check.q: What is an 'interest' in negotiation?
o: The underlying reason someone wants something

check.q: Why prepare a minimum acceptable outcome?
o: So you can ask for nothing
So you know when to say yes or walk away

check.q: Two sisters want the same orange. One needs the juice, the other the peel. What best solves it?
o: Discover interests and give each what they need
Cut it in half by weight

units.title: Week 21: Leadership Through Service
units.summary: Lead by serving: see a need, act with humility and measure whether people were really helped.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Explain servant leadership and how it differs from leading by power
• Use See, Serve, Reflect to lead a small act of service
• Identify a need in your school or community that you could address
Name someone who leads without having an official title. What makes them a leader anyway?

sections.h: True story: Walid Bial (16 years old) (Marrakech, Morocco)
p: Walid was elected as the president of his school’s youth club. He was very excited to be the leader. On his first day, he sat at the main desk, gave orders to the other students, and told them to clean up the club storage room while he checked his phone. The other students felt insulted, stopped working, and walked out of the room.
Walid was confused and went to his favorite teacher for advice. The teacher told him, "A true leader is not a boss who sits on a throne. A true leader is the person who grabs the broom first."

The next afternoon, Walid apologized to the group. He put on old clothes, grabbed a trash bag, and started scrubbing the dirty floor himself. Seeing their president working hard, the other students laughed, grabbed their brooms, and joined in happily. Walid learned that real leadership is not about power or status; it is about serving your team and leading by example.
Can you lead without having an official title? How?
Who is someone who leads through service, in your own life?
What is one way you could serve your class or community this month?

Leadership is not a title; it is influence used for good. Servant leadership, a term coined by Robert Greenleaf, flips the usual picture: the leader's first job is to serve the people they lead, by listening, removing obstacles and helping others grow. The test is whether those served become healthier, wiser and more capable.

You do not need a position to lead through service. Cleaning a shared space, mentoring a younger student or organising a food drive are all leadership. Serving also builds skills you need later: planning, empathy, persuasion and humility.

b: Lead by serving: notice a need, act with humility and check that people truly benefited.

p: 1. See: look and listen for a real need, and ask the people affected what they need, rather than guessing
2. Serve: choose a small, doable action, recruit helpers and do the work without needing credit
3. Reflect: ask the people served and your team, 'Did this help? What would make it better?'
4. Repeat: improve the idea and invite others to lead the next round
The situation: Ejike notices that junior students at his school eat lunch alone on the first week of term because they do not know anyone.
How it often goes wrong: He posts a speech on social media about 'bullying' but takes no action. Nothing changes for the juniors.

b: See: he talks to three juniors, who say they feel nervous and lost
Serve: with two friends he starts a 'Lunch Buddies' table and invites juniors to join games
Reflect: after two weeks, they ask the juniors for feedback and learn that a short orientation tour also helps
Repeat: they add the tour, and a Year 9 team takes over next term.

p: Mistake: serving for applause. Fix: Focus on the impact, not the photo.
Mistake: deciding what people need without asking. Fix: Listen first.
Mistake: starting too big and burning out. Fix: Begin with a small, repeatable action.
(5 min) List three needs you see at school, at home and in your community
(10 min) Choose one and map the See, Serve, Reflect steps
(10 min) Plan a mini-project: who, what, when, how you will measure success
(5 min) Pitch it to a partner in 60 seconds
When has someone served me without expecting anything back?
Who is overlooked in my school or neighbourhood?
What does 'success' look like for a service project?
• Leadership is influence used to help others
• Ask people what they need before acting
• Measure impact by whether lives improve
Self-rating (1 to 5): How confident do I feel using this skill right now, and what is one thing that would raise my score by a point?

units.activity: This week's challenge: Complete one act of service you planned in the lab, with at least one other person involved. Collect feedback from those served and record the impact. Add your plan, evidence and reflection to your Community Service record.

check.q: What is the first job of a servant leader?
o: To serve the people they lead

check.q: Why ask people what they need before serving?
o: To avoid guessing and actually address real needs

check.q: What is the best measure of a service project's success?

units.title: Week 22: Networking
units.summary: Build genuine professional relationships by introducing yourself well, asking good questions and following up.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Explain networking as building relationships, not collecting contacts
• Prepare a 30-second introduction and two good questions
• Follow up within 48 hours and keep the relationship alive
Who is someone you'd love to have a 15-minute conversation with, and why?

sections.h: True story: Ryan Ho (16 years old) (Singapore)
p: Ryan Ho loved coding video games, but he did not know anyone in the professional gaming industry. His school arranged a field trip to a massive local technology convention. While his friends stayed in a tight group laughing and eating free snacks, Ryan decided to practice his networking skills.

He felt shy, but he forced himself to walk up to a booth run by a professional game studio. He did not ask them for a job. Instead, he introduced himself politely, smiled, and asked the lead designer a simple question: "What is the biggest mistake young programmers make when starting out?"

The designer was impressed by Ryan's politeness and curiosity. They had a great five-minute chat, and the designer handed Ryan his business card, telling him to email his game projects for feedback. By stepping out of his comfort zone to build a polite connection, Ryan opened a huge door for his future career.
Why did Walid's polite, specific email work better than a generic request?
Who is someone you admire that you could respectfully reach out to?
What makes an introduction message feel genuine rather than 'salesy'?

Networking simply means building a circle of people who know you, trust you and want to help you, and whom you also want to help. Most opportunities, such as internships, scholarships and advice, come through people. The best networkers are curious, generous and consistent, not pushy.

A good first meeting is short and genuine. You introduce yourself clearly, show interest in the other person and ask a question that invites a story. The real work happens afterwards: a thank-you message, a useful link or an update keeps the relationship alive.

b: Networking is about being curious, helpful and consistent, and following up.

sections.h: The method: Prepare, Introduce, Ask, Follow up
p: 1. Prepare: know who will be there and write a 30-second introduction (name, what you do or study, what you are curious about)
2. Introduce: smile, give a firm greeting, say your introduction and ask their name and role
3. Ask: use open questions, 'How did you get into this work?' and 'What advice would you give someone my age?'
4. Follow up: within 48 hours send a short message, 'Thank you for speaking with me. I enjoyed hearing about...'; offer something in return when you can
The situation: At a school career fair, Ope stands near the wall and speaks only when a speaker asks her a question. She leaves without any names.
How it often goes wrong: Weeks later she wants advice about engineering but knows no one to ask.

b: Prepare: 'Hi, I am Ope, a Year 10 student who loves building things. I am curious about engineering.'
Introduce: she greets the civil engineer, says her line and asks for her name
Ask: 'What did you enjoy most about your degree?'
Follow up: she sends a thank-you message on LinkedIn or email, and later shares a photo of her school project.

p: Mistake: asking for a favour immediately. Fix: Build rapport first.
Mistake: only talking about yourself. Fix: Aim for 70 per cent listening.
Mistake: never following up. Fix: Set a reminder for 48 hours.
(5 min) Write your 30-second introduction
(10 min) Practise a mini networking event: move around and talk to three people using your introduction and two questions
(5 min) Draft a follow-up message
(5 min) Share one thing you learned about a classmate
What stops me from starting conversations with new people?
Who could I help with something I know?
Who should I follow up with this week?
• Networking is relationships, not collecting contacts
• Good questions beat clever introductions
• Follow-up turns a meeting into a connection
Self-rating (1 to 5): How confident do I feel using this skill right now, and what is one thing that would raise my score by a point?

Collecting as many contacts as possible

units.title: Week 23: Cultural Intelligence
units.summary: Work effectively with people from different cultures by staying curious, learning and adapting.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Explain what cultural intelligence (CQ) is and why it matters
• Describe the iceberg model of culture: visible behaviour and hidden values
• Use the CQ cycle: Drive, Knowledge, Strategy, Action
Share one custom, food, or tradition from your own background that you're proud of.

sections.h: True story: Amara Nwosu (13 years old) (Vancouver, Canada)
p: Amara moved from a small town in Nigeria to a highly diverse school in Vancouver, Canada. On her first day, she sat next to a classmate named Yuki, who had recently moved from Japan. At lunchtime, Amara offered Yuki a piece of her savory Nigerian meat pie. Yuki took it with both hands, bowed her head slightly, and did not make any sound while eating it.

Amara thought Yuki was being rude or cold because she did not shout "Thank you!" or jump up with excitement like her friends back home would. Instead of getting upset, Amara decided to learn about Yuki's background. She discovered that in Japanese culture, showing quiet respect and using two hands to accept a gift is a sign of deep gratitude.

The next day, Amara handed Yuki a snack using both of her hands and gave a gentle bow. Yuki’s face lit up with a massive, happy smile. Amara learned that cultural intelligence means understanding that people show respect and kindness in many different ways, and taking the time to learn those differences makes the world a much friendlier place.
What is a cultural misunderstanding you've witnessed or experienced?
How do you usually learn about a culture that isn't your own?
What is one custom or perspective from another culture you find fascinating?

Culture is the shared habits, beliefs and values of a group. It shapes how people greet each other, how they treat time, how direct they are and how they show respect. Cultural intelligence (CQ) is the ability to work well across cultures by being curious, learning and adjusting your behaviour.

A helpful picture is an iceberg: above the water you see food, clothes, language and festivals; below the water sit values, beliefs and assumptions that drive them. When behaviour surprises you, ask what hidden value might be behind it. Culture also includes differences within a country, such as between regions, religions and generations.

b: Be curious, learn what is beneath the surface, plan how to adapt and act with respect.

sections.h: The method: The CQ Cycle: Drive, Knowledge, Strategy, Action
p: 1. Drive: show real interest and confidence in learning about people from other backgrounds
2. Knowledge: learn about their customs, values and communication styles from reliable sources and the people themselves
3. Strategy: before meeting, plan how you will adjust, for example how formal to be and how to greet
4. Action: adapt your behaviour respectfully, ask when unsure and reflect afterwards on what you learned

The situation: A Nigerian student joins an online project team with students from Japan, Germany and Brazil. In the first call, the Japanese student rarely speaks, the German student is very direct and the Brazilian student arrives 10 minutes late and apologises warmly.
How it often goes wrong: The Nigerian student concludes, 'The Japanese student is not interested, the German is rude and the Brazilian is lazy,' and gives them a low rating.

b: Drive: she decides to understand rather than judge
Knowledge: she learns that in some cultures people wait to be invited to speak, directness is seen as honesty and time norms vary
Strategy: she plans to invite quieter members by name and agree a start time
Action: 'Kenji, would you like to share your view?' and 'Let us agree meetings start at 5:00 with a five-minute buffer.'

p: Mistake: stereotyping a whole nation from one person. Fix: Treat each person as an individual first.
Mistake: judging others by your own norms. Fix: Ask what the behaviour means to them.
Mistake: staying silent for fear of offending. Fix: Ask respectfully; people appreciate genuine curiosity.
(5 min) Draw an iceberg for your own culture: three visible things and three hidden values
(10 min) In groups, read a cross-cultural misunderstanding case and identify the hidden values
(10 min) Plan how you would behave using the CQ cycle
(5 min) Share one insight
What do I assume is 'normal' that may not be normal elsewhere?
When did I feel excluded or misunderstood because of culture?
Which culture would I like to learn about, and how?
• Visible behaviour rests on hidden values
• Curiosity beats assumption
• Adapting is a sign of respect, not weakness
Self-rating (1 to 5): How confident do I feel using this skill right now, and what is one thing that would raise my score by a point?

units.title: Week 25: Critical Thinking
units.summary: Question claims, weigh evidence and reach conclusions you can defend.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Separate facts, opinions and assumptions in a statement
• Test a claim using the QEAC checklist: Question, Evidence, Alternatives, Conclusion
• Spot common reasoning traps such as bandwagon and false either-or
Share a claim you once believed that turned out to be false. How did you find out?

sections.h: True story: Emma Yang (16 years old) (New York City, USA)
p: Emma Yang spent a lot of time reading health articles online during her school breaks, but she soon noticed a very disturbing pattern. Dozens of websites were sharing medical stories and health advice that sounded completely fake, yet thousands of people were liking, sharing, and believing them without a second thought. Emma realized that people were blindly trusting whatever popped up on their screens because they lacked the tools to question the information. This dangerous trend made her realize that the internet needed a digital shield to help everyday citizens separate fact from fiction. Instead of just complaining about the issue, she decided to use her software programming skills to build an artificial intelligence app that could analyze online text and automatically detect fake news.

She spent months tucked away in her bedroom, typing thousands of lines of code and testing different algorithms. When she shared her idea with her high school classmates, some of them laughed and said it was completely impossible for a single teenager to outsmart professional internet liars. This skepticism did not stop Emma; instead, it pushed her to examine the problem even more closely from different angles. She collected thousands of verified real articles and compared them directly with known fake articles to find the hidden patterns in how fake news is written. Her intense research helped her train her app to look for exaggerated emotional words, unverified links, and anonymous authors that normal readers usually skip.

When major news stations heard about her invention, they invited her to speak live on television. The adult journalists on the panel asked Emma why anyone should trust a computer program written by a high school student instead of professional fact-checkers. Emma did not get defensive or nervous under the bright studio lights; she simply smiled and walked them through her logical process. She explained exactly how her code checked the source code of a website, verified the registration data of the link, and cross-referenced the claims with trusted scientific databases. By presenting clear, objective data instead of getting emotional, she completely changed the minds of the doubtful reporters and gained massive respect from top global tech executives.

Her successful presentation proved to teenagers everywhere that you do not have to accept everything you see, hear, or read at face value. Emma showed that critical thinking is not about arguing with people or being cynical; it is about slow, careful investigation and using logic to find the solid truth. Her app went on to help thousands of internet users check their sources before hitting the share button. By encouraging people to stop and ask hard questions, Emma proved that a sharp mind and a commitment to facts are the most powerful tools anyone can use to navigate the modern digital world.
What is a claim you once believed that turned out to be false?
How do you decide whether a source of information is trustworthy?
What assumption are you making about a problem you're currently facing?

Critical thinking is the habit of asking, 'How do I know this is true?' before believing or sharing something. It does not mean criticising everything; it means weighing evidence fairly and being willing to change your mind. In a world of viral posts, forwarded messages and persuasive adverts, it is a survival skill.

A claim is stronger when it comes from a reliable source, is supported by several independent pieces of evidence and still holds up when you consider other explanations. Our brains also take shortcuts, such as believing what most people believe or what fits what we already think. Knowing these traps helps us avoid them.

b: Before you believe or share a claim, question it, check the evidence and consider alternatives.

sections.h: The method: QEAC: Question, Evidence, Alternatives, Conclusion
p: 1. Question: what exactly is being claimed, who is saying it and why?
2. Evidence: what proof is given, is it reliable and can it be checked in at least two independent sources?
3. Alternatives: what other explanations could fit the facts, and who disagrees and why?
4. Conclusion: decide how confident you are (certain, probably, unsure) and say what would change your mind
The situation: A WhatsApp broadcast says, 'Drinking hot water with lemon cures all infections. Forward to 10 people to save lives.' It has a photo of a person in a white coat.
How it often goes wrong: Amaka forwards it to 15 contacts because it sounds helpful and many people have shared it.

b: Question: who wrote it and what is the exact claim: 'cures all infections'?
Evidence: she finds no named source; she searches the World Health Organization and a health ministry site and finds nothing supporting it
Alternatives: lemon water may be healthy, but it does not cure infections
Conclusion: 'Almost certainly false.' She replies to the sender with the checked facts and does not forward it.

p: Mistake: trusting a claim because many people share it. Fix: Popularity is not proof.
Mistake: only looking for evidence that agrees with you. Fix: Search for the best argument against your view.
Mistake: treating all sources as equal. Fix: Ask who benefits and who checked it.
(5 min) Sort ten statements into fact, opinion or assumption
(10 min) Take one viral claim and run the QEAC checklist in groups
(10 min) Find two independent sources for or against it
(5 min) Each group states its confidence level and what would change its mind
What have I believed or shared that turned out to be false?
Which of my opinions have I never questioned?
Whose views do I rarely listen to, and why?
• Check claims before believing or sharing
• Look for the best opposing argument
• Confidence should match the strength of evidence

o: Believe it if many people share it
Ask who says it and what evidence supports it

o: So you never reach a conclusion
Because the first explanation may not be the only or best one

units.title: Week 26: Creative Thinking
units.summary: Generate many ideas, then choose and improve the best using divergent and convergent thinking.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Explain divergent and convergent thinking and when to use each
• Use SCAMPER prompts to improve an existing product or idea
• Defer judgement during brainstorming to produce more ideas
60 seconds — how many uses can you think of for a paperclip?

sections.h: True story: Sibahle Zwane (11 years old) (Johannesburg, South Africa)
p: Sibahle Zwane absolutely loved mathematics, but his local school faced massive challenges because they did not have enough textbooks, calculators, or computers for the students. Many kids in his neighborhood felt discouraged by the lack of resources and found math classes incredibly boring. Instead of complaining about what he didn’t have, Sibahle decided to treat the entire world as his classroom. He found a very funny and highly unusual way to practice his mental skills by turning his daily walk to school into a massive math game. He began reading the random numbers printed on the license plates of passing cars and instantly multiplying or dividing them in his head before the vehicles drove out of sight.

This bizarre daily habit quickly turned Sibahle into a local legend in his neighborhood. Local shopkeepers and neighbors began standing outside their storefronts just to watch the young boy walk past and test his brain with giant math problems. A local resident eventually filmed a video of Sibahle multiplying complex three-digit numbers faster than an adult could type them into a digital smartphone. The video exploded in popularity online, gaining millions of views across the globe. Soon, representatives from a prestigious local university drove down to his neighborhood to meet him and were so amazed by his skills that they offered him a full academic scholarship for his future education.

The sudden fame did not change Sibahle's joyful attitude toward learning. One afternoon, a group of older students approached him with a smartphone calculator and challenged him to solve a massive math problem involving percentages and fractions. As a crowd gathered around to watch, Sibahle closed his eyes for a split second, danced on his toes, and shouted out the perfect answer before the smartphone screen could even finish calculating. The entire street burst into loud laughter and cheers, and the older boys shook his hand in complete disbelief. Sibahle proved to his community that creative thinking does not require expensive tools or fancy classrooms; it just requires an open imagination and the willingness to see learning opportunities in everyday objects.

His unique story inspired thousands of other children across South Africa to rethink how they viewed difficult school subjects. Sibahle showed his peers that math wasn't just a set of dry rules written in a textbook, but a living puzzle that could be played anywhere. By using his creativity to overcome a lack of resources, he opened doors for his future that his family never thought possible. He left a lasting lesson for young people everywhere that when you change the way you look at your surroundings, you can turn any ordinary street into a path toward success.
What is the wildest idea you've ever had, and what happened to it?
What blocks your creativity the most — fear of judgment, or fear of failure?
How can 'silly' ideas lead to genuinely good ones?

Creativity is not a gift only artists have; it is the ability to produce ideas that are both new and useful, and it can be practised. Creative thinking has two phases. Divergent thinking is going wide: producing as many ideas as possible without judging. Convergent thinking is narrowing: choosing, combining and improving the best ones.

Most people mix the two phases and kill ideas too early by saying, 'That will never work.' Teams that separate them, first a burst of quantity, then selection, produce better results. Prompts like SCAMPER give your brain handles to hold, so you are not staring at a blank page.

b: Go wide first (no judging), then narrow down and improve.

p: 1. Substitute and Combine: what could you replace, or what could you join with something else?
2. Adapt and Modify: what could you copy from another field, or make bigger, smaller or different?
3. Put to another use and Eliminate: who else could use this, and what could you remove?
4. Reverse or Rearrange: what if the order, role or direction were flipped? Then converge: pick the three best ideas and test them

The situation: A school wants to reduce the plastic bottles littering its field. The student council brainstorms, but the first person says, 'Just ban bottles,' and the others agree because no one wants to argue.
How it often goes wrong: Only one idea is explored, it is not popular, and the plastic keeps piling up.

b: Diverge: 30 ideas in 10 minutes without comment
Substitute: refill stations instead of bottles
Combine: a reward app that pays points for refills
Reverse: 'bottle bank' collection and recycling art
Converge: vote on three, prototype the refill station and test for a month.

p: Mistake: judging ideas while generating them. Fix: Use 'Yes, and...' during the wide phase.
Mistake: stopping at the first good idea. Fix: Aim for quantity; the best idea is often the 15th.
Mistake: only brainstorming alone. Fix: Mix solo thinking with group sharing.
(5 min) Pick an everyday object, such as a school bag
(10 min) Generate 20 SCAMPER improvements in pairs
(5 min) Converge: choose three and combine them
(10 min) Sketch and pitch the best idea in 60 seconds
When do my best ideas come to me?
What do I say that kills ideas, mine or others'?
What problem at school or home needs a creative fix?
• Diverge first, converge second
• Quantity leads to quality
• Prompts help creativity start

check.q: What is divergent thinking?
o: Producing many ideas without judging them

check.q: Why separate brainstorming from selecting ideas?
o: Early judging kills ideas before they develop

units.title: Week 27: Problem Solving
units.summary: Find the real cause of a problem and test small solutions before committing.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Define a problem clearly before looking for solutions
• Use the 5 Whys to move from symptom to root cause
• Test a solution on a small scale and learn from the results
Name a problem you solved recently, even a small one. How did you approach it?

sections.h: True story: Reyhan Jamalova (17 years old) (Baku, Azerbaijan)
p: Reyhan Jamalova grew up in a city that frequently experienced intense, heavy rainstorms that caused major disruptions. These massive downpours often overwhelmed the local electrical grid, leading to sudden blackouts that left hundreds of families sitting in the dark without heating or internet. While most people simply complained about the bad weather and waited for the power company to fix the lines, Reyhan began to look at the falling rain differently. She wondered why the city was letting millions of gallons of fast-moving water go to waste when that kinetic energy could potentially be captured and turned into clean electricity for the community. When she shared her idea with her school science teacher, he shook his head and told her the concept was far too complicated to build without an expensive laboratory.

Reyhan refused to let a lack of money stop her from trying to solve the energy problem. She spent her weekends searching through local junkyards and her family’s garage, gathering old plastic plumbing tubes, broken toy motors, and scraps of copper wire. She set up a temporary workspace in her backyard and spent months building a unique, mechanical device that she named Rainergy. Her plan was simple: the device would collect pouring rainwater from roof gutters, funnel it down a narrow tube to increase its speed, and use that fast water to spin a tiny toy motor that generated electrical currents. Her goal was to create a cheap, portable system that poor families could easily set up outside their homes during storms to keep their lights on.

However, her very first public test in her backyard turned into a complete disaster. A sudden blast of storm wind caught the lightweight plastic frame of her prototype, smashing it against the ground and breaking her carefully soldered copper wires into pieces. Water leaked all over her tools, and her device lay ruined in the mud while the rain kept pouring down. Reyhan did not cry or throw her tools away in frustration; instead, she laughed at the messy situation, dried off her hands, and carried the broken pieces back to her desk. She used thicker plastic tubes and stronger glue to rebuild the frame, making it tough enough to withstand severe weather.

The next time a major storm hit the city, Reyhan stood under an umbrella in her backyard and watched the water rush through her newly rebuilt device. Within seconds, the tiny LED light bulb attached to the generator flickered to life and shone with a brilliant, steady glow. Her persistent problem-solving skills had successfully turned a frustrating weather disaster into a useful source of clean, free energy. Reyhan proved to teenagers worldwide that real problem solving is not about getting everything right on the first try; it is about studying your failures, fixing your mistakes, and refusing to quit until you find a practical answer to the challenge in front of you.
What is a real problem in your school or community that bothers you?
What is the real root cause, versus the surface symptom?
What would a first, small test of a solution look like?

Problem solving is more than finding answers; it starts with asking the right question. Many solutions fail because they fix the symptom, not the cause. If you keep mopping up a leaking roof without finding the hole, you will mop forever.

Good problem solvers work in loops: define the problem precisely, dig for root causes, generate options, try a small test, and learn from what happens. Small experiments are cheaper and safer than big bets, and they turn a scary problem into a series of learnable steps.

b: Define it, dig to the root cause, test small, then scale what works.

sections.h: The method: Define, Dig, Design, Test
p: 1. Define: write the problem in one sentence with who, what and how you know, such as '40% of Year 9 students submit homework late'
2. Dig: ask 'Why?' up to five times until you reach a cause you can act on
3. Design: list at least three possible solutions and pick one to test
4. Test: try it small for a short time, measure the result and adjust
The situation: A community group notices that the local borehole keeps running dry. They plan to ask for a second borehole.
How it often goes wrong: They spend months raising funds for a new borehole, which runs dry too, because the real cause was never found.

b: Define: 'The borehole runs dry by 10 am daily for the past month'
Dig: Why? Pump runs all day. Why? Tank leaks. Why? A cracked pipe. Why not fixed? No one is responsible for maintenance
Design: three options: repair the pipe, appoint a caretaker, install a timer
Test: repair the pipe, appoint a caretaker and measure water levels for two weeks.

p: Mistake: jumping to solutions. Fix: Spend time defining the problem.
Mistake: blaming people instead of processes. Fix: Ask what in the system allowed this.
Mistake: launching a big solution untested. Fix: Pilot with a small group first.
(5 min) Choose a real school or community problem
(10 min) Write a clear problem statement and do a 5 Whys chain
(10 min) Brainstorm three solutions and design a small test with a measure
(5 min) Present your chain to another group for challenge
What problem do I keep 'solving' without success?
Who could help me see the root cause?
What small experiment can I run this week?
• A well-defined problem is half solved
• Root causes beat quick fixes
• Small tests reduce risk

o: To move from a symptom to a root cause

units.title: Week 28: Decision Making
units.summary: Make better decisions with clear options, criteria and a check for regret and risk.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Use a decision matrix to compare options against weighted criteria
• Tell reversible from irreversible decisions and set the right effort level
• Apply the 10-10-10 test to reduce emotional decision-making
Describe a decision you're currently torn about (nothing too private).

sections.h: True story: Autumn Peltier (17 years old) (Ontario, Canada)
p: Autumn Peltier found herself facing a massive personal dilemma that kept her awake for days. Because of her incredible work as an environmental activist, she received an official invitation to fly across the world and give a major speech about clean water protection at a massive international conference. However, when she looked at her calendar, she realized with a heavy heart that the conference fell on the exact same weekend as her high school basketball championship game. Autumn had practiced with her basketball team all year, and her teammates were counting on her to help them win the regional trophy. She felt completely torn down the middle between her loyalty to her friends and her duty to her community.

To help her navigate this stressful situation, Autumn decided to step back from her emotions and make a logical list of the long-term impact of both choices. She realized that while the basketball game would be an absolute blast, the excitement would only last for one single afternoon. On the other hand, her speech at the global conference would be heard by powerful world leaders who had the direct authority to create new laws protecting clean drinking water for thousands of indigenous children. By weighing the short-term fun against the long-term value, she made the incredibly mature decision to pass up the championship game and board the plane to the conference.

When the day arrived to tell her basketball coach and her teammates about her final choice, Autumn’s stomach was full of nervous knots because she was terrified that they would think she was selfish. Instead of getting angry, her coach gathered the entire team in the gym and handed Autumn a basketball that every single player had signed with encouraging messages for her trip. As Autumn walked out onto the massive international stage a few days later, she felt a wave of fear looking at the crowd of adults in expensive suits. She took a deep breath, pictured the signed basketball in her mind, and delivered a powerful speech that brought the entire auditorium to its feet for a standing ovation.

Her viral speech helped raise thousands of dollars for clean water filters, proving that her difficult decision had achieved exactly what she hoped. Autumn learned that good decision making does not mean choosing the easiest path or trying to make absolutely everyone happy at the same time. It means aligning your choices with your deepest values and having the courage to stick to your purpose, even when it means missing out on temporary fun. Her journey showed teenagers everywhere that making thoughtful choices today is the only way to build a meaningful impact for tomorrow.
What is the hardest decision you've had to make recently?
How do you usually decide when you're torn between two good options?
What happens when you avoid making a decision at all?

Every day you make decisions, from small ones like what to eat to big ones such as choosing subjects. Good decisions are not always good outcomes; they are choices made with the best information and reasoning you had. Decisions go wrong when we rush, follow the crowd or ignore what matters to us.

A simple structure helps: list real options, decide what criteria matter most, score each option and check the result against your gut feeling. Also ask whether a decision is reversible. A reversible decision, like trying a club, can be made quickly. An irreversible one, like leaving school, deserves much more care and advice.

b: List options, weigh what matters, test the result, and spend more time on decisions you cannot undo.

sections.h: The method: Options, Criteria, Weigh, Test
p: 1. Options: list at least three real options, including 'do nothing' and a creative option
2. Criteria: choose four to five things that matter (cost, interest, future use, effect on family) and weight each from 1 to 5
3. Weigh: score each option on each criterion, multiply by the weight and add up the totals
4. Test: ask the 10-10-10 question: how will I feel about this in 10 minutes, 10 months and 10 years? Then decide and set a date to review
The situation: Bayo must choose between Physics, Economics and Art as his optional subject. His friends are choosing Economics, and his uncle says, 'Take Physics, it is serious.'
How it often goes wrong: He picks Economics because friends are there, then struggles because he does not enjoy numbers and it does not match his goal of designing buildings.

b: Options: Physics, Economics, Art, and 'trial two lessons of each'
Criteria: interest (weight 5), link to architecture (5), difficulty (3), friends (1)
Weigh: Art and Physics score highest; Economics scores low
Test: 10-10-10 shows he would regret not choosing a subject linked to his dream. He picks Physics and keeps drawing as a club.

p: Mistake: deciding only when emotional. Fix: Sleep on it when possible.
Mistake: considering only two options. Fix: Add a third, creative option.
Mistake: treating all decisions as life-or-death. Fix: Decide quickly on reversible choices.
(5 min) Write a real decision you face
(10 min) Build a decision matrix with four criteria and weights
(10 min) Run the 10-10-10 test and compare it with the matrix result
(5 min) Discuss with a partner what the matrix revealed
What was my best decision and what made it good?
Do I decide mostly on feelings, friends or facts?
Which pending decision needs more information?
• Process improves decisions
• Weights show what really matters to you
• Reversible choices deserve speed, irreversible ones deserve care

units.title: Week 29: Ethics
units.summary: Reason through ethical dilemmas and build a personal ethical standard you can explain.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Identify who is affected by each option in a dilemma
• Use three tests: Who is affected? What if everyone did this? Could I explain it to someone I respect?
• Explain the difference between ethics and simply following rules
What's a rule you think should exist that currently doesn't?

sections.h: True story: Anand Krishna Mishra (11 years old) (Lucknow, India)
p: Anand Krishna Mishra spent his evenings running a completely free outdoor school in his local village for poor children whose families could not afford basic school supplies or uniforms. He gathered the kids under a large tree every afternoon, using his own small allowance to buy a few pencils and notebooks for them to share. A wealthy local business owner noticed the massive crowds of children attending Anand's classes and walked up to him with a stunning offer. The businessman opened a briefcase filled with a massive stack of money and said he would gladly pay for all the school books, desks, and supplies Anand could ever dream of owning.

However, Anand quickly realized that this generous offer came with a very uncomfortable ethical catch. The businessman explained that in exchange for the money, Anand had to force all the poor children to wear shirts featuring the company’s large corporate logo. Furthermore, the businessman wanted to bring professional photographers to the school every week to take pictures of the smiling, poor kids holding up his products to use in online advertisements. The businessman wanted to use the children’s poverty to make his corporation look kind and charitable so he could sell more products to rich customers.

Anand sat alone under the teaching tree that night, looking at his worn-out pencils and thinking about the massive fortune he had just been offered. He knew that taking the money would make his life incredibly easy, but his inner moral compass screamed at him that using poor, vulnerable children as living billboards was deeply wrong and unfair to their dignity. The next afternoon, the eleven-year-old boy met with the wealthy businessman, looked him directly in the eye, and politely turned down the entire fortune. He stated that his students were human beings who came to learn, not commercial advertisements to be bought and sold for corporate profit.

The businessman was furious and mocked Anand, warning him that without corporate money, his little tree school would run out of supplies and fail completely within a month. Anand remained calm and replied that honesty and respect were worth much more than a pile of deceptive money. Word of the young boy’s incredible integrity spread rapidly through the city, touching the hearts of local college students and retired teachers. Within weeks, dozens of volunteers showed up at the tree with donations of books, chalkboards, and their own time to teach for free. By choosing ethical principles over easy money, Anand built a trusted community school that succeeded because it was founded on true honor and mutual respect.
Describe a situation where the 'easy' choice and the 'right' choice were different.
What ethical line would you never cross, no matter the pressure?
How do you decide what's fair when people disagree?

Ethics is about deciding what is fair and right using consistent principles, not just following what is comfortable or what the loudest person suggests. Real dilemmas are rarely 'right versus wrong'; they are often 'right versus right', where two things you value pull in different directions.

There is not always one agreed 'correct' answer to an ethical problem, but there is better and worse reasoning. Good reasoning considers everyone affected, tests the choice against fairness ('what if everyone did this?') and is honest enough to be explained in public. Ethical courage means holding the standard when it is inconvenient or costly.

b: Weigh who is affected, test the choice as a universal rule, and be ready to explain it openly.

sections.h: The method: The Three Ethics Tests
p: 1. Who is affected: list everyone touched by each option and how seriously
2. What if everyone: imagine all people in a similar situation made this choice; would the world be better or worse?
3. Explain it: could you explain your choice, calmly and honestly, to someone whose judgement you respect, or to a newspaper reader?
4. Decide and own it: choose, accept the cost, and learn from what happens

The situation: Ruth finds a wallet with 15,000 naira and an ID card in the school corridor. Her friend says, 'Keep it, whoever lost it is careless.' Ruth's family has struggled to pay school fees this term.
How it often goes wrong: Ruth keeps the money, then feels anxious for weeks every time she sees the owner, a junior student, asking about it.

b: Who is affected: the junior student, her family, her own conscience, the school community
What if everyone: if everyone kept found money, no one could trust others
Explain it: she knows she would be ashamed to tell her teacher she kept it
Decide: she hands the wallet to the office and later receives a small reward and a thank-you from the student's parent.

p: Mistake: using 'everyone does it' as a justification. Fix: Popularity does not make something right.
Mistake: hiding behind rules. Fix: Understand why a rule exists and when it fails.
Mistake: thinking ethics is for important people. Fix: Practise in small daily choices.
(5 min) Read a dilemma card and write your first instinct
(10 min) Discuss in groups using the three tests; each person speaks before debate
(10 min) Prepare and present your group's reasoning, not just the answer
(5 min) Note whether anyone changed their view and why
What ethical line would I never cross, and why?
When did the easy choice and the right choice differ for me?
Whose opinion helps me reason well?
• Ethical reasoning weighs everyone affected
• Test choices as if everyone did the same
• Courage means keeping standards when it costs something

o: A choice between two obviously different options

units.title: Week 30: Project Management
units.summary: Plan and deliver a project with clear scope, tasks, timeline, risks and review points.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Define the scope and success measure of a project in one paragraph
• Break work into tasks with owners and deadlines
• Identify two risks and plan to handle them
What's the biggest project you've ever organised (a party, a trip, a group assignment)?

sections.h: True story: Dasia Taylor (19 years old) (Iowa City, Iowa, USA)
p: Dasia Taylor made an incredible scientific breakthrough when she invented a special type of medical thread that changed its color from purple to bright pink to alert doctors if a patient's surgical wound was infected. She was highly motivated to present her brilliant invention at a massive national science fair, but she faced a massive problem: she only had three weeks left before the final entry deadline. Her laboratory desk was a complete disaster area, covered in loose research papers, chemical bottles, testing dishes, and tangled wires. Dasia felt a wave of panic wash over her because the sheer volume of work left to do made her feel completely frozen and overwhelmed.

She realized that if she kept working without a clear structure, she would run out of time and fail to finish her project. She decided to clear off a section of her wall and set up a physical project management board using a pack of colorful sticky notes. She drew three simple columns on the board and labeled them To Do, Doing, and Done. She then broke her massive scientific project down into dozens of tiny, individual tasks, writing each one on a separate note. Instead of stressing about the entire three-week deadline, she promised herself that she would only look at the notes she placed in the Doing column each morning.

This step-by-step strategy was put to the test during her second week of intense lab work when she suddenly ran out of an essential chemical solution. In the past, this kind of unexpected mistake would have caused her to panic and lose an entire afternoon to worry. Because she had an organized project board right in front of her, she quickly looked at her columns and moved a written report task forward instead. She spent the rest of the day typing out her background research while waiting for the new chemical delivery to arrive the following morning. Her structured approach kept her calm, focused, and completely in control of her limited time.

By breaking her giant mountain of work into organized, daily steps, Dasia completed her medical invention with two days to spare and took home the top prize at the national exhibition. She proved to young people everywhere that project management is not just a boring corporate skill for adults; it is an essential tool that protects your mind from stress. Dasia showed that even the biggest, most complicated goals in life can be achieved smoothly if you have the discipline to break them down into an organized track of tiny, manageable tasks.
What is a project you've completed that you're proud of? How did you organise it?
What usually causes your projects to run late?
What tool or habit could help you track progress better?

A project is a temporary effort with a clear goal, a deadline and limited resources. From organising a school fair to launching a small business, projects succeed when someone plans them, tracks progress and adjusts. Planning is not paperwork; it is thinking ahead so that problems appear on paper rather than on the day.

Four ideas keep projects on track: scope (what is in and what is out), tasks and owners (who does what by when), risks (what could go wrong and what we will do) and review (regular check-ins). The MoSCoW method helps prioritise: Must have, Should have, Could have, Will not have this time.

b: Scope it, break it into tasks with owners and dates, plan for risks and review regularly.

sections.h: The method: Scope, Tasks, Risks, Review
p: 1. Scope: write the goal, the deliverable, the deadline and what is out of scope; sort features using MoSCoW
2. Tasks: list every task, assign an owner and a due date, and order them on a simple timeline
3. Risks: list the top two or three risks, rate them, and write a backup, such as 'If the venue cancels, we use the school hall'
4. Review: hold a 10-minute check-in each week to update progress and fix blockers
The situation: A student club promises to hold a career day in three weeks. They discuss ideas excitedly but do not write anything down.
How it often goes wrong: Nobody books speakers until week 2, the hall is double-booked and the event is cancelled the day before.

b: Scope: a two-hour career day with three speakers, 100 students, on the 20th; out of scope: food
Tasks: Ada books the hall by Monday; Tunde invites speakers by Wednesday; Zainab prepares the programme by Friday
Risks: speaker drops out, so keep two backups; hall clash, so book a second room
Review: short Friday check-ins to update a shared task list.

p: Mistake: making plans that no one owns. Fix: Give every task a name and a date.
Mistake: adding more and more features. Fix: Protect the Musts and say no to extras.
Mistake: planning no slack. Fix: Add a buffer for delays.
(5 min) Choose a mini-project, such as a class quiz or charity drive
(10 min) Write the scope and apply MoSCoW
(10 min) Create a task list with owners and dates
(5 min) Identify two risks and backups
Which project of mine went wrong, and what plan could have saved it?
Am I better at starting or finishing?
What project would I love to lead this year?
• Scope protects focus
• Tasks need owners and dates
• Risks are easier to handle when planned

units.title: Week 31: Leadership Styles
units.summary: Learn leadership styles and adapt your approach to the person and the situation.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Describe four leadership styles: directing, coaching, supporting and delegating
• Match a style to a team member's skill and motivation
• Identify your default style and one style to practise
Describe a leader you've had (coach, teacher, captain) who got the best out of you. What did they do?

sections.h: True story: Khin Sandar (15 years old) (Yangon, Myanmar)
p: Khin Sandar was absolutely thrilled when her high school classmates voted for her to serve as the lead director of the school’s annual drama play. She wanted the performance to be absolutely perfect, so she decided to adopt a very strict, bossy leadership style on her very first day of rehearsals. She stood in the center of the stage, blew a loud whistle, and began shouting direct orders at everyone, refusing to let anyone else speak. She unilaterally chose the costumes, rewrote lines without asking the actors, and told the stage crew exactly how to paint the scenery without listening to their input.

This commanding approach backfired on Khin within less than a single week. Her classmates felt insulted, unappreciated, and deeply frustrated by her refusal to listen to their voices, so they began showing up late to rehearsals and text-messaging each other instead of practicing. The acting looked wooden, the stage crew stopped painting, and the entire play felt like a sinking ship. Khin sat alone in the empty auditorium one evening, staring at the messy stage and realizing that acting like an angry dictator was destroying the team's spirit and ruining her dream.

She made the brave decision to completely change her leadership style from an authoritarian boss to a collaborative leader before the next rehearsal started. When the students gathered the next afternoon, Khin sat down on the floor with them in a circle, apologized for her arrogant behavior, and placed a blank notebook in the middle. She asked the artistic students to sketch out their own ideas for the scenery, allowed the actors to suggest funny changes to the script, and gave everyone a shared vote on the final costume designs. The energy in the room transformed instantly, and the students began staying late and working hard because they finally felt valued.

During the actual opening night performance, a major crisis hit when one of the main actors accidentally dropped a crucial prop on stage and froze in total terror under the bright lights. Because Khin had spent weeks building a supportive, creative team environment instead of a culture of fear, the other actors did not panic or wait for orders. Another student quickly stepped forward, improvised a brilliant, funny line that incorporated the dropped prop, and saved the entire scene smoothly. The audience clapped loudly, and Khin realized that a great leader’s job is not to command a group of servants, but to lift up and empower a team of confident problem solvers.
Which leadership style do you naturally lean toward?
Describe a leader you admire — what style do they use?
When might a directive style be necessary, even if it's less popular?

There is no single best way to lead. Situational leadership, developed by Paul Hersey and Ken Blanchard, suggests that the best style depends on the person and the task. A beginner who is eager needs clear direction; an experienced but discouraged person needs support; a skilled, confident person needs freedom.

Many young leaders have one default, such as bossing everyone or avoiding any conflict. Effective leaders learn to flex. They diagnose how skilled and motivated each person is for this particular task and choose the right balance of direction and support.

b: Match your leadership style to the person's skill and motivation for the task.

sections.h: The method: Four Styles: Direct, Coach, Support, Delegate
p: 1. Direct: for low skill, high enthusiasm, give clear instructions, show how and check often
2. Coach: for some skill, lower confidence, explain why, ask questions and give encouragement
3. Support: for high skill, variable confidence, listen, encourage and let them decide how
4. Delegate: for high skill and high confidence, agree the goal and step back, offering help if asked
The situation: Ope leads a school radio team: Kayode is brand new, Sade is talented but upset after criticism, and Ife has produced the show for two years.
How it often goes wrong: Ope gives everyone the same long instructions and is quick to correct. Kayode gets confused, Sade withdraws, and Ife feels micromanaged.

b: Kayode: direct, with a step-by-step checklist and a buddy
Sade: support, with praise for specific strengths and a chance to decide her segment
Ife: delegate, with the goal 'produce the Friday show' and a check-in only if needed
Ope reviews each person's progress weekly and adjusts.

p: Mistake: using one style for everyone. Fix: Diagnose each person and task.
Mistake: delegating to a beginner without support. Fix: Teach first, then delegate.
Mistake: micromanaging experts. Fix: Agree outcomes and trust them.
(5 min) Read four short team member profiles and match each to a style
(10 min) Role-play giving the same instruction in two different styles
(10 min) Complete a quick self-assessment of your default style
(5 min) Choose one style to practise this week
Which leaders helped me grow, and what style did they use?
What is my default style and what is its risk?
Who needs a different style from me?
• No single style fits everyone
• Skill and motivation guide the choice
• Flexible leaders get more from teams
