units.title: Week 32: Leading Teams
units.summary: Lead a team with a shared vision, clear roles, healthy meetings and psychological safety.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Write a one-sentence team vision that people can repeat
• Run a 15-minute meeting with an agenda, decisions and actions
• Create psychological safety so that people can speak up without fear
What's the hardest part of getting a group of people your own age to actually do something together?

sections.h: True story: Tobi, Chinedu, and Amina (16 years old) (Abuja, Nigeria)
p: Tobi felt a massive weight of responsibility on his shoulders when he was named the captain of his high school’s competitive debate team. They had successfully made it all the way to the national championship finals, but behind the scenes, the team was completely fracturing into small, hostile groups that refused to speak to each other. Chinedu, who was an incredibly fast talker, kept bragging that he was the smartest speaker on the team and didn't need anyone's help. Meanwhile, Amina, who was quiet but brilliant at researching facts, felt that her detailed notes were being completely ignored by the louder boys. Tobi knew that if they didn't unite as a solid family immediately, they would face an embarrassing defeat on the national stage.

Instead of picking sides or shouting at his teammates to get along, Tobi decided to handle the conflict by organizing a casual surprise lunch at a local restaurant outside of school. Once the food arrived, Tobi explicitly banned all talk about debate topics for thirty minutes and instead asked each person to share one personal fear they had about the upcoming competition. Amina nervously admitted that her hands shook whenever she had to deliver an opening speech, and Chinedu surprised everyone by confessing that he actually hated doing research because he struggled to organize data under pressure. Hearing these honest vulnerabilities completely changed how the teammates viewed each other.

Tobi used this new understanding to completely reorganize how the team functioned, matching their roles to their hidden personal comfort zones. He asked Chinedu to focus entirely on delivering the passionate closing arguments using Amina’s perfectly organized research data, and he placed himself in the middle to support them both. This shift made everyone feel incredibly safe, respected, and appreciated for their unique strengths. The awkward silence disappeared, replaced by laughing and shared strategy sessions as they worked together as a synchronized unit.

This deep bond saved them when a massive emergency occurred right as they walked onto the main championship stage. Chinedu’s clip-on microphone suddenly broke, and he began to panic as the judges called his name to speak. Without a single second of hesitation, Amina unclipped her own working microphone, stepped forward with a calm smile, and held it up for him so they could share it. Their incredible coordination and calm teamwork absolutely amazed the judging panel and earned them maximum points for unity and leadership. Tobi watched them from the front row, proud that his effort to bring them together over a simple lunch had turned a group of isolated rivals into a legendary championship team.
What is the difference between managing a team and leading one?
How would you motivate a teammate who has lost interest in a project?
What is the hardest part of leading people your own age?

Leading a team means helping a group of different people work toward the same goal. Research by Google on its own teams found that the most important factor in high-performing teams was psychological safety, a shared belief that it is safe to ask questions, admit mistakes and share ideas without being humiliated.

Leaders build this with simple habits: a clear vision, defined roles, short and purposeful meetings, fair recognition and a calm response to mistakes. How a leader reacts the first time someone admits an error decides whether anyone ever admits one again.

b: Give your team a clear vision, regular rhythm, fair recognition and a safe place to speak up.

sections.h: The method: Vision, Roles, Rhythm, Recognition
p: 1. Vision: write one sentence the whole team can repeat, 'We will give every Year 7 student a friend by Friday.'
2. Roles: make sure everyone knows their part and who decides what
3. Rhythm: hold a short, regular meeting with an agenda, decisions recorded and next steps assigned
4. Recognition: thank people specifically and respond to mistakes with 'What can we learn?' instead of blame
The situation: Amina leads the science club. In meetings she speaks most of the time, rolls her eyes at weak ideas and becomes angry when a member forgets the equipment.
How it often goes wrong: Members stop sharing ideas, and two quit. Amina thinks, 'They are not committed.'

b: Vision: 'Every member runs one experiment this term.'
Roles: a rota for equipment, with a backup
Rhythm: a 15-minute weekly meeting with a written agenda, everyone speaks once before anyone speaks twice
Recognition: 'Thanks, Yusuf, for the great demo.' When equipment is missing: 'What can we change in the rota?'

p: Mistake: dominating the talk. Fix: Ask quiet members first.
Mistake: criticising in public. Fix: Give corrections privately and praise publicly.
Mistake: long meetings without decisions. Fix: Use an agenda and finish with actions.
(5 min) Write a vision sentence for a real group you lead or could lead
(10 min) Draft a 15-minute meeting agenda
(10 min) Run a mock meeting where the leader practises inviting quiet voices
(5 min) Discuss how mistakes were handled
How do I react when someone admits a mistake?
Do people feel safe speaking up around me?
What recognition would motivate my team?
• Psychological safety is the foundation of strong teams
• Vision, roles and rhythm keep a team aligned
• Specific recognition motivates

check.q: What is psychological safety?
o: A belief that you can speak up or admit mistakes without being humiliated

check.q: Which makes a meeting more effective?
o: A clear agenda, decisions and action list

check.q: A member admits a mistake. The best leader response is:
o: Ask what can be learned and how to fix it

units.title: Week 33: Digital Citizenship
units.summary: Behave responsibly, respectfully and safely online and protect your digital footprint.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Explain what a digital footprint is and why it lasts
• Apply the THINK test before posting: True, Helpful, Inspiring, Necessary, Kind
• Respond to online unkindness by documenting, blocking, reporting and telling a trusted adult
If a stranger only saw your social media, what would they assume about you?

sections.h: True story: Alex Walker (14 years old) (London, United Kingdom)
p: Alex Walker was relaxing in his living room when he noticed a notification pop up on his school’s public social media group page. A student from the junior class had accidentally tripped and scored a goal against his own team during a massive lunchtime football match. Dozens of older students had started posting mean comments, embarrassing photos, and cruel jokes mocking the poor boy's mistake. Alex found one of the memes incredibly funny and immediately saved it to his phone, getting ready to repost it with his own sarcastic comment so he could get cheap likes and look cool in front of his online friends.

Right as his thumb hovered over the upload button, Alex paused and remembered an important lesson he had learned about digital footprints. He realized that once something is posted on the internet, it can never truly be deleted, and it becomes a permanent part of your digital reputation. He took a close look at the meme and thought about how he would feel if hundreds of people were laughing at him online after a bad day. He realized that joining in the online mockery wouldn't make him cool; it would just make him a digital bully who contributed to someone else's pain.

Alex deleted the mean meme from his phone and decided to use his digital voice to change the direction of the conversation. He opened a private chat window and sent a supportive message directly to the upset junior student, saying, "Don't stress about today, everyone makes mistakes and you are still an awesome football player." He then went back to the public group page and used the reporting tool to flag the bullying comments to the school's online website moderator. Within an hour, the mean posts were completely removed from the page, and the toxic online argument came to a sudden halt.

The following morning at school, the junior student quietly walked up to Alex in the crowded hallway and thanked him with a look of immense relief. He confessed to Alex that those mean online comments had kept him awake crying all night until Alex's kind private message arrived and gave him the courage to come to school. Alex felt a massive wave of personal satisfaction and realized that true digital citizenship is about responsibility and empathy. He learned that the words people type behind a glowing glass screen have real-world power, and being a good digital citizen means using that power to protect people instead of tearing them down.
What would a stranger assume about you from your social media alone?
What is something you posted that you later regretted, or almost posted?
What does 'responsible digital citizen' mean to you?

Digital citizenship means using technology responsibly, respectfully and safely. Everything you post, like, comment on or search leaves a trail called your digital footprint. Universities and employers often search for candidates online, and screenshots can travel further than you ever intended.

The internet also feels anonymous, which can make people cruel or careless. Remember that there is a real person behind every screen. Respect, privacy and kindness online matter as much as they do in the school yard, and the consequences can be bigger because content spreads and lasts.

b: Treat your online life like a permanent, public record: think before you post and be kind.

sections.h: The method: THINK Before You Post
p: 1. True: is it accurate, or am I sharing a rumour?
2. Helpful and Inspiring: does it help or encourage someone?
3. Necessary: does it need to be said, and does it need to be said publicly?
4. Kind: would I say this to their face, and would I be comfortable if my parents or a future employer read it?
The situation: After a football loss, Tayo posts a rude meme mocking a teammate's mistake. It gets many likes. The teammate stops coming to practice.
How it often goes wrong: Tayo says, 'It was only a joke,' but the post is screenshotted, shared and later seen by the coach and some parents.

b: He pauses and applies THINK: not kind, not necessary
He deletes the post, apologises privately and shares the team's supportive message instead
If he receives mean messages about his own mistakes, he screenshots, blocks, reports and tells his coach.

p: Mistake: believing deleted means gone. Fix: Assume anything posted can be saved.
Mistake: sharing private details such as your school, address or location. Fix: Keep personal information private.
Mistake: joining pile-ons. Fix: Do not like or share unkind posts; support the target privately.
(5 min) Search your name (or a made-up student name) and discuss what a stranger would learn
(10 min) Review five sample posts and apply the THINK test
(10 min) Role-play responding to an unkind comment and to a friend who posted something harmful
(5 min) Write three personal rules for your online life
What would I be embarrassed for my future boss to see?
Do I behave differently online than offline, and why?
Who would I tell if I felt unsafe online?
• Your digital footprint lasts
• THINK before you post
• Report and support when you see harm

o: The trail of data and posts you leave online

units.title: Week 34: Digital Literacy
units.summary: Use digital tools effectively: search smartly, judge information, organise work and create and share.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Search with precise keywords and operators to find reliable information
• Evaluate a website using the CRAAP checklist: Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose
• Use basic documents, spreadsheets and cloud storage to organise and share work
How do you currently decide if something you read online is true?

sections.h: True story: Sarah Lim (15 years old) (Singapore)
p: Sarah Lim was busy working on her school history essay when her smartphone buzzed with an incoming text message that grabbed her attention. The message featured the official colors and logo of her school administration and claimed that she had been randomly selected to receive a brand-new digital tablet. To claim her free prize, the text stated that she needed to click a link immediately, type in her home address, and enter her personal school portal password to verify her identity. Sarah felt a huge rush of excitement and immediately clicked the link, getting ready to type in her private data so she wouldn't miss out on the incredible offer.

Right as she placed her fingers on the keyboard, her digital literacy training kicked in, and she told herself to slow down and check the screen carefully. She noticed that the website link looked incredibly long and messy, containing weird symbols instead of the official school website address. She scrolled back up to the original text message and saw that the word "Administration" was spelled with a slight typo that a real school office would never make. Sarah realized that this was not an official notification from her teachers, but a highly dangerous phishing scam designed by internet hackers to steal her private login passwords.

Instead of typing her information or panicking, Sarah took a screenshot of the scam message and walked straight down to the principal's office to report it. The school technology director confirmed that hackers were targeting students that afternoon and thanked Sarah for her sharp eyes and quick thinking. The principal was so impressed by her digital literacy that she asked Sarah to give a presentation about online safety to her entire homeroom class the following morning. Sarah felt incredibly proud as she stood at the chalkboard, showing her classmates the exact red flags she had discovered on her phone.

She explained to her friends that online thieves always use urgent language and exciting prizes to make people act quickly without thinking. Many of her classmates looked shocked and admitted that they would have easily fallen into the trap and typed their passwords if they had received that same message. By sharing her digital knowledge, Sarah did not just protect her own family’s private data; she kept her entire class safe from cybercriminals. She proved to her peers that digital literacy is not just about knowing how to type fast or use social media apps, but about knowing how to analyze information safely so you can stay one step ahead of online dangers.
How can you tell a credible source from an unreliable one?
What is a piece of misinformation you've seen spread online?
What research habit would make you a more effective digital learner?

Digital literacy is the ability to find, evaluate, create and communicate information using technology. Being able to scroll quickly is not the same as being digitally literate. Many young people are confident users but weak at judging reliability or using tools for productivity.

Searching well is a skill: specific keywords, quotation marks for exact phrases and the right site types (such as .edu or .gov) give better results. Evaluating what you find matters even more, because anyone can publish anything. Finally, productive tools such as documents, spreadsheets and cloud folders help you organise work, collaborate and never lose a project.

b: Find it well, check it carefully, create something useful and share it responsibly.

sections.h: The method: Find, Evaluate, Create, Share
p: 1. Find: use specific keywords, quote exact phrases and try more than one search engine or source
2. Evaluate: check Currency (how recent), Relevance, Authority (who wrote it), Accuracy (can it be verified) and Purpose (to inform, sell or persuade)
3. Create: turn information into something useful: notes, a spreadsheet, a chart, a short presentation, in your own words
4. Share: store files with clear names, use cloud folders and share links with the right permissions
The situation: Halima needs facts on renewable energy in Nigeria for a presentation. She types 'energy' into a search engine and copies the first result.
How it often goes wrong: The result is an old blog post from a seller of solar panels. She presents outdated numbers and loses marks.

b: Find: 'renewable energy Nigeria 2025 statistics' with quotation marks around 'renewable energy'
Evaluate: choose a government agency and a university report, checking dates and authors
Create: record figures in a spreadsheet and make one chart in her own words
Share: save to a cloud folder named 'Energy Presentation', set to 'view only' for classmates.

p: Mistake: trusting the first result. Fix: Compare at least two reliable sources.
Mistake: copying and pasting. Fix: Summarise in your own words and cite sources.
Mistake: poor file names ('final final 2'). Fix: Use clear names with dates.
(5 min) Practise three searches with different keywords on the same question
(10 min) Evaluate two web pages using CRAAP
(10 min) Create a simple spreadsheet with three columns and make a chart
(5 min) Save, name and share the file with view permissions
Where do I usually get information, and how reliable is it?
Which digital tool could save me the most time?
How do I organise my files, and what could improve?
• Smart searching saves time
• CRAAP helps judge reliability
• Create and share thoughtfully

units.title: Week 35: AI & Responsible Technology
units.summary: Use AI as a smart assistant while staying honest, accurate and in charge of your own thinking.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Explain in simple terms what generative AI can and cannot do
• Write a clear prompt using Role, Task, Context, Format
• Verify AI output, protect private data and state when you used AI
Where have you already used an AI tool, knowingly or not?

sections.h: True story: Gitanjali Rao (19 years old) (Colorado, USA)
p: Gitanjali Rao was deeply concerned about the rising problem of online bullying, so she decided to use her advanced coding skills to build an artificial intelligence tool called Kindly. Her goal was to create a smart program that teenagers could install on their phones to automatically scan text messages and flag mean or harmful language before it was sent. However, as she began training the AI's brain, she quickly realized that building advanced technology came with massive ethical dangers. She discovered that if she only trained the AI on a small set of standard words, the computer might accidentally misunderstand friendly slang, miss actual hidden bullying, or unfairly flag harmless jokes between close friends.

She realized that if her AI program made too many mistakes, it could cause massive misunderstandings, ruin teenage friendships, and lose the trust of the people it was built to protect. Instead of rushing to launch her app immediately to become famous in the tech world, Gitanjali chose to slow down and act responsibly. She spent weeks gathering data from diverse cultural backgrounds, checking various teenage dialects, and testing thousands of phrases from around the world. She worked tirelessly to ensure that the AI was completely fair, balanced, and accurate before it was released to the public.

During a massive technology convention in California, a professional software engineer asked Gitanjali if checking every single cultural phrase slowed down her development progress and cost too much time. Gitanjali looked at the adult audience and confidently replied that building a safe, fair tool slowly is always much better than launching a broken technology fast that ends up hurting innocent people. The room fell silent as the adult engineers realized that this teenager possessed a deeper understanding of technology ethics than many major corporations. Her responsible approach inspired several software companies to review their own AI code for hidden biases and errors.

Gitanjali proved to young programmers everywhere that building the technology of the future is not just about making cool features or making money; it is about protecting human dignity. She showed that responsible technology requires empathy, patience, and a constant willingness to double-check your work for unintended consequences. By prioritizing safety and fairness over speed and fame, she built a highly successful tool that genuinely helped teenagers communicate safely. She left a powerful example that the ultimate goal of technology should always be to serve and protect humanity.
Where have you already used AI tools, knowingly or not?
What is a responsible way to use AI for schoolwork? What crosses a line?
What worries you most about AI's role in the future?

Generative AI tools can write, summarise, translate and brainstorm, but they predict plausible words; they do not 'know' things and can state falsehoods confidently, a problem often called hallucination. They can also reflect biases in the data they learned from. That makes them powerful assistants and risky authorities.

Responsible use has three habits: be clear about what you want, always verify important facts, and be honest about when you used AI, following your school's rules. Never paste private information such as passwords, ID numbers or other people's personal details into a tool. The aim is to think better with AI, not to stop thinking.

b: Use AI as a co-pilot: prompt clearly, verify everything important, protect privacy and be honest about its use.

sections.h: The method: Prompt, Verify, Protect, Disclose
p: 1. Prompt: give a Role ('act as a tutor'), Task ('explain photosynthesis'), Context ('for a 14-year-old') and Format ('in five bullet points')
2. Verify: check key facts, numbers and quotes in reliable sources; ask the tool for sources and then confirm they exist
3. Protect: never share passwords, personal data or private images, and be careful with uploaded files
4. Disclose: say when and how you used AI, and do your own thinking; follow school and exam rules
The situation: Nkechi is told to write a short report on the history of the Nigerian railway. She asks an AI to 'write it' and submits what it gives her.
How it often goes wrong: The report contains two invented dates and a made-up quotation. Her teacher notices and gives a zero for dishonesty.

b: Prompt: 'Act as a history tutor. Give me an outline of the main periods of Nigerian railway development for a 15-year-old, as five bullet points.'
Verify: she checks each date in a library book and a reputable encyclopaedia
Protect: she does not include personal details
Disclose: she writes the report herself, uses the outline and notes, 'I used an AI tool to help plan the outline and verified all facts.'

p: Mistake: copying AI output as your own. Fix: Use it to learn and draft, then write in your own words and say you used it.
Mistake: trusting confident answers. Fix: Verify facts and ask for sources.
Mistake: sharing sensitive data. Fix: Treat prompts as public.
(5 min) Write one vague prompt and one improved prompt using Role, Task, Context, Format
(10 min) Compare outputs and mark anything that may be wrong
(10 min) Verify two claims using reliable sources
(5 min) Draft a one-sentence AI-use disclosure
Where could AI help me learn, and where could it harm my learning?
What would I never put into an AI tool?
How do I feel about work I did with AI compared with work I did alone?

• Clear prompts give better help
• Verify, protect and disclose

units.title: Week 36: Cyber Safety
units.summary: Keep yourself and your accounts safe from scams, phishing and weak security.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Recognise phishing and common online scams in messages and links
• Create a strong password and turn on two-factor authentication
• Apply Stop, Look, Verify before clicking, paying or sharing
What's one cyber-safety habit you already practise?

sections.h: True story: Michael Mwangi (13 years old) (Nairobi, Kenya)
p: Michael Mwangi absolutely loved playing online multiplayer video games on his family's computer after finishing his school homework every afternoon. One day, while he was in the middle of an intense match, a player he had never met before sent him a private message offering an incredible deal. The stranger claimed to be a professional game developer and offered to send Michael thousands of free virtual game coins and rare character skins completely for free. Michael felt an immediate rush of excitement because these virtual items usually cost a lot of real money that he did not have.

However, the online stranger then explained that to complete the transfer, Michael needed to do two simple things immediately. The stranger asked Michael to take a quick photo of his mother's credit card from her purse and type in the exact name and street address of his school so they could verify his account location. Michael's heart began to beat fast, and he almost reached for his mother's wallet because the temptation to get the free game coins was incredibly strong. But right as he picked up his phone, he remembered a serious cyber safety lesson his teacher had shared during a school assembly.

He remembered that online criminals frequently pretend to be friendly gamers and offer exciting rewards just to trick kids into giving away private family financial details. Michael realized that if he shared that photo, he could allow a complete stranger to steal his family's money and find out exactly where he went to school every day. He kept his cool, closed the chat window immediately, and used the game's safety tools to block the user forever. He then walked into the living room and told his parents exactly what had happened at his desk.

His father praised Michael for his incredible maturity and immediately checked the computer to make sure no dangerous tracking software had been downloaded. Michael felt an immense sense of relief that he had controlled his desires and resisted the temptation of the free offer. He realized that cyber safety is not about missing out on gaming fun or being paranoid; it is about setting strong personal boundaries to protect your home and family from real-world dangers hiding behind a digital screen.
What is a cyber-safety habit you already practise, and one you should start?
Have you or someone you know encountered an online scam? What happened?
What would you tell a younger sibling about staying safe online?

Cyber criminals prefer to trick people rather than hack machines, because it is easier. Phishing messages pretend to be from your bank, a prize organiser or a friend, and push you to click quickly, often with urgency such as 'Your account will be closed in 24 hours'.

You can reduce most risks with a few habits: strong, unique passwords (ideally a long phrase), a password manager if possible, two-factor authentication, updated devices and careful checking of links and senders. If something feels too good to be true or too urgent, it usually is.

b: Slow down, check the sender and link, use strong passwords and two-factor protection.

p: 1. Stop: pause when a message creates urgency, fear or excitement; scammers want you to act before thinking
2. Look: check the sender's address, spelling, odd links and requests for passwords, codes, PINs or payment
3. Verify: contact the organisation through its official website or number, not through the message; ask an adult
4. Protect: use a long unique password phrase, turn on two-factor authentication and report or delete the message
The situation: Ikenna gets an SMS: 'Congratulations! You won 500,000 naira. Click here and enter your bank details to claim.' He is excited because his family could use the money.
How it often goes wrong: He clicks, enters his details and later finds that money is missing from his parent's account.

b: Stop: he notices the urgency and that he never entered a contest
Look: the link is not an official bank domain, and it asks for his PIN
Verify: he tells his parents and calls the bank using the number on the card
Protect: they delete and report the message and change a password that was reused.

p: Mistake: reusing one password everywhere. Fix: Use unique passwords or a password manager.
Mistake: sharing one-time codes. Fix: Never give codes to anyone, even someone claiming to be the bank.
Mistake: clicking to 'see what happens'. Fix: Verify first.
(5 min) Spot the red flags in five sample messages
(10 min) Create a password phrase of four random words and test its strength on a checker (without entering the real password)
(10 min) Turn on or plan two-factor authentication for one account
(5 min) Role-play calling a bank or a parent to verify a message
Have I or someone I know been tricked online?
Which of my accounts has the weakest protection?
Who would I tell if I made a mistake online?
• Scammers use urgency and emotion
• Strong passwords and 2FA block most attacks
• Verify using official channels

units.title: Week 37: Personal Branding
units.summary: Build a personal brand that is honest, consistent and backed by proof of your skills.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Explain personal branding as the reputation you build, not self-promotion
• Write a brand statement using Values, Strengths, Story, Proof
• Create a short, consistent online profile or bio
If you had to describe yourself in a three-word 'headline', what would it be today?

sections.h: True story: Meisa Salama (16 years old) (Vancouver, Canada)
p: Meisa Salama had a huge dream of studying photography at a prestigious university after she graduated from high school. She decided to look at her existing personal social media pages to see how an admissions director might view her online presence. To her complete shock, she realized that her profiles were an absolute mess, filled with blurry photos of her lunch, random internet jokes, and angry complaints about her difficult school teachers. Meisa suddenly realized that if a university professor looked her up online, they would think she was lazy, disorganized, and completely unprofessional.

She understood that her digital footprint was creating a false impression of her true talents, so she decided to completely rebuild her personal brand from scratch. She spent an entire afternoon deleting her negative rants, removing the embarrassing photos, and cleaning up her profile descriptions. She then started using her pages as a beautiful digital portfolio, sharing only her absolute best wildlife and nature photography. She added short, positive captions to each post, explaining the camera settings she used and the creative lessons she learned while taking each shot.

At first, some of her close school friends began to tease her, asking why her page looked so professional and why she stopped posting funny memes. Meisa just laughed at their jokes and told them that she was actively investing in her future career instead of just wasting time online. Within less than six months, the editor of a local Canadian photography magazine stumbled across her clean, professional page and was so impressed by her consistent brand that she invited Meisa to shoot a local public event.

When Meisa eventually applied to her dream university, the admissions board explicitly praised her thoughtful online presence and awarded her a creative scholarship. Her school friends were amazed and quickly asked Meisa for personal advice on how to clean up their own messy social media accounts. Meisa showed them that your personal brand is your digital introduction to the world, and taking the time to showcase your best skills, values, and passions online can turn a casual internet hobby into incredible real-world opportunities.
If your personal brand were a headline, what would it say today?
What do you want to be known for in five years?
How does your online presence support (or contradict) that?

Your personal brand is what people say about you when you are not in the room. You already have one; the question is whether you shape it on purpose. A strong brand is honest: it is built from your real values and strengths, shown consistently, and backed by proof such as projects, results and references.

In the digital world, people will often meet your brand online first. Consistency matters: your tone, photo and message across platforms should tell the same story. Authenticity matters more: a brand built on exaggeration collapses at the first meeting.

b: Know your values and strengths, tell your story and show proof, consistently and honestly.

sections.h: The method: Values, Strengths, Story, Proof
p: 1. Values: choose two or three values you want to be known for (from Week 5)
2. Strengths: pick two or three strengths with evidence (from Week 3)
3. Story: write a short story or line that shows these in action (from Week 16)
4. Proof: gather evidence, such as a project, certificate, testimonial or portfolio piece, and write a short bio such as 'I am a curious student who uses coding to solve community problems.'
The situation: Joy is applying for a youth leadership programme. Her social media is full of jokes at others' expense, and her bio says, 'No filter, no regrets.'
How it often goes wrong: The selectors see an unfocused and sometimes unkind profile and doubt her maturity.

b: Values: kindness and curiosity
Strengths: organising and public speaking
Story: she started a reading club for neighbourhood children
Proof: photos of the club, a letter from a teacher and a short bio. She clears out harmful posts and updates her bio: 'Joy, 15. Reading-club founder. Curious about people and ideas.'

p: Mistake: pretending to be someone else. Fix: Be your best self, not a fake self.
Mistake: inconsistent messages across platforms. Fix: Align photo, tone and bio.
Mistake: no proof. Fix: Show projects and results.
(5 min) Write three words you want others to use about you
(10 min) Complete the four steps and draft a one-sentence brand statement
(10 min) Write a 50-word bio for a profile
(5 min) Swap with a partner and check whether the proof supports the claims
What would my friends, teachers and family say is my brand?
Which online content does not match who I want to be?
What proof could I gather this term?
• Your brand is your reputation, so shape it
• Consistency builds trust
• Proof beats claims

units.title: Quarter 3 Capstone: Innovation Challenge
units.summary: Design and defend a specific, workable solution to a real-world problem using everything you practised this quarter.

p: By the end of this capstone you will be able to:
• Define a real problem clearly and propose one specific solution
• Show evidence of research, creativity and ethical thinking in your pitch

What real-world problem, big or small, would you most like to fix?

Thirteen weeks of sharpening how you think, critically, creatively, ethically and digitally, lead to one test: can you design an actual, workable response to a real-world problem, not just describe it?

The Innovation Challenge draws on design thinking: a problem clearly defined (Week 25), a range of options considered (Week 26), one solution developed and defended, tested if possible with users (Weeks 27 and 41).

Strong pitches go beyond describing a problem. They commit to a specific solution, show how it could work in practice, give honest limits and consider who could be affected, using ethics (Week 29) and digital skills (Weeks 33 to 36).

b: Real-world problem statement
Designed solution or prototype
Presentation to peers

When you receive feedback, write it down without defending yourself, then choose one change to make.

units.title: Week 39: Financial Literacy
units.summary: Understand how money works: earn, spend, save, give, and protect yourself from financial traps.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Tell needs from wants and plan a simple monthly budget
• Explain how saving, interest and inflation affect the value of money over time
• Spot common money traps such as pyramid schemes and get-rich-quick offers
What's the best (or worst) money decision you've seen someone make?

sections.h: True story: Jose Adolfo Quisocala (16 years old) (Arequipa, Peru)
p: Jose Adolfo Quisocala noticed that many of his high school classmates were spending all their pocket money on plastic toys and sweet snacks every single day, leaving them with absolutely zero savings for important things like school books or future university fees. At the same time, he saw a massive amount of plastic bottles and old cardboard trash cluttering the streets of his hometown. Jose realized that his peers lacked a basic understanding of financial planning and environmental care. He decided to find a highly unusual way to solve both problems at once by launching a student bank called the Eco-Banco, where children could open real savings accounts using solid trash instead of coins.

His classmates were highly confused at first and laughed at the idea of bringing garbage to a bank teller. Jose patiently set up a system where kids brought plastic bottles, old newspapers, and used cardboard to the bank kiosk, which was then weighed and sold directly to recycling recycling companies. The money earned from the trash was automatically deposited into each student's personal savings account as real currency. Jose designed a rule that prevented the students from touching their funds until they reached a specific savings goal, teaching them the core financial habit of delayed gratification and patience.

As the months passed, the students stopped buying cheap candy and began competing to see who could gather the most recyclable materials after school. One afternoon, a student named Mario came to the kiosk with a massive sack of plastic bottles hoping to withdraw all his cash to buy a video game. Jose sat down with him, pulled out a simple notebook, and showed him how keeping his money in the account for another three months would allow him to afford a much better laptop for his upcoming high school exams. Mario laughed, realized the long-term value of waiting, and chose to leave his money in the bank to grow.

Through this unique eco-bank, over 2,000 young students learned how to budget their earnings, manage independent accounts, and invest in their future while cleaning up thousands of tons of local street pollution. Jose’s brilliant system caught the attention of international organizations, and he was flown to Europe to receive prestigious global awards for youth finance. He proved to teenagers everywhere that financial literacy is not just a boring topic for adult businessmen; it is a practical superpower that allows you to take control of your resources, protect your community, and build real independence from a young age.
What is the biggest money mistake you've seen someone make (or made yourself)?
How do you currently decide between spending and saving?
What would you do with an unexpected windfall of money?

Money is a tool, not a goal. Financial literacy means understanding how to earn it, spend it wisely, save for the future, give generously and avoid traps. Habits formed as a teenager, such as saving something from every income, often last a lifetime.

Two ideas surprise most people. Compound interest means your savings earn money on the money they have already earned, so starting early matters more than starting big. Inflation means prices rise over time, so money kept idle loses buying power. Offers that promise huge returns with no risk are almost always scams.

b: Pay yourself first, plan before you spend, let time work for you and avoid anything that promises easy riches.

sections.h: The method: Earn, Spend, Save, Give
p: 1. Earn: list every source of income, such as allowance, gifts, small jobs or a business
2. Spend: sort spending into needs and wants; plan with a simple rule, for example 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings and giving, adjusted to your situation
3. Save: pay yourself first by moving savings out as soon as money arrives; set a clear target, such as an emergency fund
4. Give and protect: set aside something to share; check any investment offer: who regulates it, can I withdraw, and does it promise guaranteed high returns?
The situation: Femi earns 10,000 naira a month from tutoring younger children. A friend says, 'Put it in this online scheme: double your money in 2 weeks, guaranteed!'
How it often goes wrong: Femi invests 10,000 naira. After one week, the platform disappears and the money is gone.

b: Earn: 10,000 naira monthly
Spend: 5,000 on needs (transport, data), 3,000 on wants, 2,000 saved and given
Save: transfer 1,000 naira to a savings account on payday and 1,000 for an emergency fund
Protect: he checks the scheme, finds no regulation and a guaranteed double, which is a classic scam warning, and refuses.

p: Mistake: spending first and saving what is left. Fix: Pay yourself first.
Mistake: borrowing for wants. Fix: Wait and save, or find a cheaper option.
Mistake: believing 'guaranteed' high returns. Fix: Higher return means higher risk; guaranteed riches are a red flag.
(5 min) List your income and your top five regular expenses
(10 min) Draw a simple monthly budget with needs, wants and saving
(10 min) Calculate how 2,000 naira saved monthly grows over a year (with and without interest) and discuss
(5 min) Spot the red flags in three sample investment ads
What does money mean to me, and what messages did I learn at home?
Which spending is a want pretending to be a need?
What am I saving for, and by when?
• Pay yourself first
• Time and compounding help early savers
• Guaranteed fast riches are a scam warning

units.title: Week 40: Entrepreneurship
units.summary: Turn a real problem into a simple business idea and test it with real customers.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Describe a customer problem, a solution, a price and a way to reach customers
• Calculate simple profit: revenue minus costs
• Run a low-cost test of the idea with at least five potential customers
What everyday annoyance could actually be a business idea?

sections.h: True story: Htet Myet Aung (15 years old) (Yangon, Myanmar)
p: Htet Myet Aung looked around his neighborhood and noticed that many local students were struggling to pass their high school science exams because their textbooks were full of dry, boring text without any helpful pictures. Htet was a decent artist and loved science, so he saw a massive business opportunity to create short, colorful comic books that explained difficult scientific formulas through funny stories. He spent his entire winter break drawing his first sample booklet, but when he showed it to his older brother, he was told that nobody would pay real money for hand-drawn school notes.

Undeterred by the negative feedback, Htet decided to take a calculated entrepreneurial risk by using his small birthday savings to print fifty physical copies of his first science comic book. He walked up to his classmates during lunchtime, smiled, and offered them the booklet for a very low price. Within less than two hours, every single copy was completely sold out, and dozens of other students were knocking on his classroom door asking to pre-order the next edition. Htet realized that he had successfully identified a real community demand and created a valuable product to solve it.

As his small business began to grow rapidly, Htet faced a major operational challenge because he could not keep up with the printing demands and shipping logistics by himself. Instead of panicking or shutting down his operations, he hired three of his artistic friends, offering them a fair share of the profits to help him color the pages and deliver the booklets to local schools. He learned how to calculate printing costs, manage his weekly business budget, and handle customer feedback politely when some pages had minor ink smudges.

His tiny lunch-break project quickly transformed into a legitimate youth publishing company that provided colorful, affordable educational materials to hundreds of students across Yangon. Htet proved to young people everywhere that entrepreneurship is not about waiting until you have a giant corporate office or a massive bank account; it is about keeping your eyes open for everyday problems, taking action to create a smart solution, and learning how to manage your resources as a team to turn an idea into a thriving reality.
What everyday problem could become a business idea?
What is the smallest possible version of that idea you could test this week?
What is the biggest risk in starting something new — and how could you reduce it?

Entrepreneurship means spotting a problem and creating value for people, often for money, sometimes for social good. Many successful businesses started as small experiments by people who noticed a real need. You do not need a big idea or lots of money; you need a customer who cares enough to pay or use it.

The biggest mistake new entrepreneurs make is building too much before asking anyone. The lean approach is: talk to customers, build the smallest version that could work, test it, and improve. A business that cannot cover its costs is a hobby, so understanding revenue, costs and profit is essential.

b: Start with a real problem, test the smallest version with real customers and watch your costs.

sections.h: The method: Problem, Customer, Solution, Test
p: 1. Problem: describe one real problem and who has it, for example 'Students in my area struggle to print assignments'
2. Customer and solution: say exactly who will buy, what you will offer and why it is better than the alternative
3. Numbers: set a price and work out costs, then profit = revenue minus costs
4. Test: sell or demonstrate to five people before spending big; ask for honest feedback and adjust
The situation: Gbenga notices that his neighbours in a block of flats wait a long time for a fruit seller who comes only on Saturdays. He imagines a grand fruit app.
How it often goes wrong: He spends two months and a lot of money building an app before asking neighbours, then finds that they prefer ordering on WhatsApp.

b: Problem: neighbours want fresh fruit on weekdays
Customer and solution: weekly fruit boxes delivered by him and a friend, ordered by WhatsApp
Numbers: box sells at 3,000 naira, costs 2,000, profit 1,000 per box
Test: he offers five boxes this week, collects feedback, then adjusts the price and the box size.

p: Mistake: ignoring costs. Fix: Count everything, including your time.
Mistake: loving your idea more than customers' needs. Fix: Ask customers and listen.
Mistake: waiting for perfect. Fix: Test the smallest version quickly.
(5 min) List three problems you see around you
(10 min) Pick one and complete Problem, Customer, Solution, numbers
(10 min) Plan a five-person test and a simple script of questions
(5 min) Pitch your idea in 60 seconds
Which problem do I care about enough to work on?
Who would be my first five customers?
What am I afraid of in starting a business?
• Start with a customer's problem
• Test small before spending big
• Profit equals revenue minus costs
Self-rating (1 to 5): How confident do I feel using this skill right now, and what is one thing that would raise my score by a point?

units.title: Week 41: Design Thinking
units.summary: Solve problems for real people using the five design thinking stages.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Name the five design thinking stages: Empathise, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test
• Interview a user and capture a clear 'how might we' question
• Build a cheap prototype and improve it from feedback
What's a product or service you use every day that was clearly designed with the user in mind?

sections.h: True story: Neo Hutiri (26 years old, but his methodology is perfect for youth training) (Johannesburg, South Africa)
p: Neo Hutiri noticed a major crisis at his local community healthcare clinic that caused immense frustration for elderly patients. People suffering from chronic illnesses had to stand in massive, exhausting outdoor queues for up to three hours just to pick up their monthly prescription medications from the pharmacy windows. Neo spent an entire morning sitting outside the clinic, observing the patients, and interviewing them about their daily struggles. He realized that the core problem wasn't a lack of medicine, but an inefficient distribution system that wasted people's valuable time and energy.

Instead of rushing to build a random, expensive computer app that the elderly patients wouldn't know how to use, Neo applied the five steps of the Design Thinking process. First, he empathized with the patients by listening to their stories, then he defined the specific problem as a lack of quick, independent access to pills. In the ideation phase, he ignored traditional ideas and thought completely outside the box, sketching a concept for a secure, automated locker system that worked exactly like an ATM machine but dispensed medicine instead of cash.

He built a very simple, low-cost prototype using cardboard boxes and basic electronic locks to test how easy it was for people to enter a secure pin code. During his first test run at the clinic, several elderly users struggled to read the tiny numbers on the prototype screen because the text font was far too small. Neo did not look at this as a failure; he took the feedback, returned to his workshop, and redesigned the screen with giant, bright buttons and added local audio instructions to make it simple for everyone.

His finalized invention, called the Pelebox, completely transformed the local healthcare system by reducing medicine collection times from three hours down to under thirty seconds. Neo proved to students worldwide that design thinking is the ultimate problem-solving framework for the future. He showed that you don't need to guess what the world needs; you simply need to empathize with real people, define their exact struggles, brainstorm creative ideas, build quick prototypes, and test them repeatedly until you create a product that changes lives.
Whose problem are you trying to solve, and have you actually listened to them?
What would a 'quick and rough' first prototype of your idea look like?
What did testing your idea teach you that thinking alone couldn't?

Design thinking is a human-centred way to solve problems, popularised by Stanford's d.school. Instead of starting with a solution, you start with people: you observe, ask and listen to understand what they really need, and then create and test options with them.

The stages are not a straight line; you may loop back as you learn. A prototype can be a drawing, a cardboard model or a role-play, anything that lets you test an idea cheaply. The aim is to fail early and cheaply so that you succeed later.

b: Understand the person, define the problem, create many ideas, build quickly and test with real users.

sections.h: The method: Empathise, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test
p: 1. Empathise: observe and interview real users to learn what they do, think and feel
2. Define: write a 'how might we' question, such as 'How might we help junior students find the library quickly?'
3. Ideate: generate many ideas, then choose one or two to try
4. Prototype and Test: build a rough version, put it in front of users, watch, listen and improve
The situation: A group of students wants to reduce queues at the school canteen. They quickly decide to buy a card-payment machine.
How it often goes wrong: After spending the money, they find the queues are caused by the canteen layout, not the payment method.

b: Empathise: they watch the queue for three days and interview students and staff
Define: 'How might we help students order and collect food faster in the 20-minute break?'
Ideate: pre-order slips, a two-lane system, a pickup shelf
Prototype and Test: they try pre-order slips with one class for a week, measure time saved and adjust.

p: Mistake: designing for yourself. Fix: Talk to the real users.
Mistake: falling in love with the first idea. Fix: Make several prototypes.
Mistake: building complete products before testing. Fix: Use paper and cardboard first.
(5 min) Pick a user (a classmate, parent or teacher) and a small problem in their day
(10 min) Interview them with five open questions
(10 min) Write a 'how might we' question and sketch three ideas
(5 min) Create a simple paper prototype and test it with another group
Whose problem would I like to understand better?
What assumption did I make that the user corrected?
What is the cheapest way to test my idea?
• Start with people, not solutions
• Prototypes make ideas testable
• Test early, learn fast

A 'how might we' question helps you:
o: Frame a problem as an opportunity to explore

units.title: Week 42: Career Exploration
units.summary: Explore careers by matching interests, strengths, values and the real world of work.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Use interests, skills, values and the job market to shortlist three careers
• Learn how to research a career using at least three sources
• Prepare questions for an informational interview with a professional
What job did you want to do when you were 8 years old? Do you still want it?

sections.h: True story: Maya Verma (15 years old) (London, United Kingdom)
p: Maya Verma felt a massive wave of anxiety whenever her high school teachers asked her what specific career she wanted to pursue after graduation. Her parents wanted her to become a traditional medical doctor, her school friends were all rushing into computer programming, and her career counselor told her to pick a single path immediately. Maya felt completely stuck because she loved drawing creative artwork but also possessed a deep fascination with biology and human anatomy. She mistakenly believed that she had to pick one single interest and throw the other one away forever to find a successful job.

Instead of forcing herself to pick a random career path that she hated, Maya decided to spend a month doing thorough career exploration online. She began researching unique industries where science and art naturally crossed paths, looking at professional interviews and daily job descriptions on global career websites. She discovered an incredible, lesser-known profession called Medical Illustration, where specialized artists create the detailed diagrams and 3D organ models used by surgeons and university students in medical textbooks.

To test out if this career path actually matched her real-world skills, Maya reached out to a professional medical illustrator on an online networking platform and asked if she could shadow them during a virtual workday. She spent an afternoon watching the illustrator use digital software to transform complex brain scans into beautiful, easy-to-understand educational animations for children's hospitals. Maya watched the screen in total awe and realized that she didn’t have to compromise her identity or limit her potential to fit into a traditional box.

By taking the time to explore multiple industries instead of rushing into a random choice, Maya found a career path that perfectly blended her passion for art with her love for science. She proved to teenagers everywhere that career exploration is not about making a final, scary choice at age fifteen; it is about staying curious, researching hidden industries, and exploring how your unique mix of talents can fit into the changing job market of tomorrow.
What career have you never considered but might actually suit you?
Who could you talk to who works in a field you're curious about?
What does 'success' in a career mean to you personally?

Choosing a career is not one big decision made at 17; it is a series of experiments. The best way to decide is to gather information: what do people actually do all day, what skills and education are needed, what does it pay, and how might the job change because of technology?

Think in four circles: what you enjoy (interests), what you are good at (skills), what matters to you (values) and what the world needs and pays for (market). Where they overlap is a good place to explore. An informational interview, a short conversation with someone doing the job, is one of the best research tools you have.

b: Explore, don't guess: match yourself to the world of work and talk to people doing the job.

sections.h: The method: Interests, Skills, Values, Market
p: 1. Interests and Skills: list what you enjoy and do well, using your Strengths Triangle from Week 3
2. Values: list what matters most to you in work, such as helping people, creativity, security or income
3. Market: research three careers: tasks, training, pay, demand and future trends from at least three sources
4. Test: arrange an informational interview, a job shadow or a small project to try the work
The situation: Samuel says he wants to be a doctor because his uncle is one and everyone says it is prestigious. He has never watched a doctor work or talked to one about the training.
How it often goes wrong: He enters a science stream, struggles in Biology and feels trapped because he never explored alternatives.

b: Interests and Skills: he enjoys helping people and is good at explaining and solving puzzles
Values: meaningful work and steady income
Market: he researches medicine, physiotherapy and health technology, learning about training length and demand
Test: he interviews a physiotherapist and spends a day at a clinic, then adjusts his subjects.

p: Mistake: choosing only for prestige or pay. Fix: Match values and strengths.
Mistake: relying on one source. Fix: Use at least three, including a person in the job.
Mistake: thinking the decision is final. Fix: Treat it as an experiment you can adjust.

units.title: Week 43: CV & Personal Statements
units.summary: Write a clear, honest CV and personal statement that show your impact, not just your duties.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Structure a one-page CV with contact details, profile, education, experience and skills
• Write achievement bullets using Action verb + What + Result
• Write a personal statement that tells your story and links to a goal
What's an achievement you're proud of that you've never put on paper?

sections.h: True story: Liam Tremblay (16 years old) (Montreal, Canada)
p: Liam Tremblay wanted to apply for a highly competitive summer youth leadership program run by a major international charity in his city. The application form required him to submit a professional Curriculum Vitae (CV) and a one-page personal statement explaining why he deserved a spot in the program. Liam sat at his computer staring at a completely blank screen for hours, feeling completely discouraged because he had never held a real, paying job before. He thought his CV would look completely empty and that the judges would reject him instantly because he lacked formal office experience.

He decided to ask his older sister for advice, and she gave him a smart tip: "Your CV shouldn't just list paying jobs; it should showcase your real-world skills, your responsibilities, and your personal character." Liam took a deep breath, opened a fresh document, and began writing down his unpaid life experiences. He listed his time as the captain of his school football team, explaining how he organized weekly practices, and added his experience volunteering to clean up his local neighborhood park on weekends.

When he sat down to type his personal statement, he avoided using boring, generic phrases like "I am a hard worker who likes leadership." Instead, he wrote a genuine story about a time when his school sports team lost a major game, describing how he kept his teammates calm and encouraged them to practice harder instead of fighting. He chose clean, professional formatting, used action verbs to describe his school projects, and spent an afternoon carefully checking the text to fix any hidden spelling errors or typos.

When the charity directors reviewed his application, they skipped past older applicants with formal jobs and chose Liam because his personal statement showed incredible maturity and honesty. Liam proved to teenagers everywhere that a CV is not about bragging about a long list of expensive jobs; it is about organizing your personal experiences clearly to show your true value. He learned that a powerful personal statement tells your unique story with pride and proves to the world that you have the skills to handle future responsibilities.
What accomplishment are you proudest of that belongs on a CV?
How do you turn an ordinary experience into a compelling line on a CV?
What makes a personal statement sound authentic rather than generic?

A CV (curriculum vitae) is a short summary of who you are and what you can do. Employers or admissions officers often read it for under a minute, so clarity and relevance matter more than length. A personal statement adds the story behind the facts: why you want this opportunity and what makes you suited to it.

The strongest CVs show impact, not duties. 'Responsible for the school club' tells little; 'Led a 12-member debate club and increased attendance from 5 to 20 members in one term' shows a result. As a young person, you can include school projects, volunteering, leadership roles, sports, languages and digital skills.

b: Show impact with action verbs and numbers, keep it to one page, and tailor it to the opportunity.

p: 1. Collect: list your experiences: projects, clubs, jobs, volunteering and awards
2. Write bullets: begin with an action verb, say what you did and add the result or number: 'Organised a book drive that collected 150 books for a local library'
3. Structure: contact details, a two-line profile, education, experience and activities, skills, references on request, all on one page with clean formatting
4. Tailor and proofread: adjust for each opportunity and have someone check spelling and facts
The situation: Amaka applies for a youth internship. Her CV says, 'I am hardworking and responsible' and lists 'Member of school choir' with no details.
How it often goes wrong: The recruiter sees no evidence and moves on to a more specific CV.

b: Profile: 'Year 11 student with a passion for community education and strong organising skills'

Bullets: 'Organised a weekend reading club for 15 primary pupils for six months'; 'Raised 25,000 naira for school supplies through a bake sale'; 'Sang in the school choir and led warm-ups for 30 members'
Skills: Microsoft Word, public speaking, Igbo and English
She asks her teacher to proofread and tailors it to the internship's focus on education.

p: Mistake: lists of duties with no results. Fix: Add numbers and outcomes.
Mistake: spelling errors and inconsistent formatting. Fix: Proofread twice and ask a friend.
Mistake: unprofessional email addresses. Fix: Use a simple name-based email.
(5 min) List five experiences and one result for each
(10 min) Write three achievement bullets using Action + What + Result
(10 min) Draft a 100-word personal statement
(5 min) Swap with a partner for a proofread and one improvement
What have I achieved that I forget to mention?
What story do I want my personal statement to tell?
Whom can I ask for a reference?

• Impact beats duties
• Tailor and proofread

units.title: Week 44: Interview Skills
units.summary: Prepare for and perform well in interviews using research, STAR stories and good questions.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Research an organisation and role before an interview
• Answer behavioural questions using the STAR method: Situation, Task, Action, Result
• Ask two thoughtful questions at the end and close the interview well
What's the most awkward question you've ever been asked?

sections.h: True story: Alyssa Martinez (17 years old) (Austin, Texas, USA)
p: Alyssa Martinez was incredibly excited when she passed the first round of applications for an internship at a major local technology firm, but her excitement quickly turned into pure terror when she received an email inviting her to a live, formal interview with three company managers. Whenever Alyssa got nervous, her voice would drop to a quiet whisper, her hands would shake uncontrollably, and she would repeat the word "um" over and over again. She felt completely terrified that she would freeze up under pressure, forget her answers, and embarrass herself completely in front of the adult panel.

To prepare for the big meeting, Alyssa decided to treat the interview exactly like a sports match that required intense physical practice. She asked her mother to sit across from her at the kitchen table and act like a strict company manager, firing common interview questions at her without warning. During their first practice run, Alyssa talked so fast that her mother couldn't understand a single sentence, and she kept looking down at her shoes instead of making eye contact. Her mother laughed gently, told her to take a deep breath, and reminded her to pause for two seconds before answering each question.

Alyssa spent the next week practicing her posture, learning how to give a firm handshake, and recording her voice on her phone to make sure she was speaking loudly and clearly. She researched the technology company’s recent projects online so she could ask them a smart question at the end of the interview. On the morning of the meeting, she dressed in neat clothes, sat up perfectly straight in her chair, and focused on using the STAR method (Situation, Task, Action, Result) to structure her answers based on her school projects.

When the managers asked her to describe a time when she faced a major challenge, Alyssa did not panic or hesitate; she paused, smiled, and calmly explained how she managed a difficult group project in her chemistry class. The interviewers were thoroughly impressed by her clear speech, her calm body language, and her confident preparation, and they offered her the internship that afternoon. Alyssa proved that interview skills are not a magical talent that people are born with; they are a set of practical habits that anyone can master through slow, steady preparation and mock practice.
What interview question scares you the most, and why?
How would you answer 'tell me about yourself' in 60 seconds?
What is one question you should ask the interviewer?

An interview is a conversation where both sides check whether there is a good fit. Interviewers want to know three things: can you do the job, will you do it, and will you fit in? You answer these by showing preparation, giving specific examples and being honest and positive.

Most interviews include behavioural questions such as 'Tell me about a time you worked in a team'. The STAR method gives a simple structure: describe the Situation, the Task, the Action you took and the Result. Preparing three or four STAR stories in advance means you can adapt them to almost any question.

b: Research, prepare three STAR stories, ask good questions and show your personality.

sections.h: The method: STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result
p: 1. Situation: set the scene briefly, 'In Year 10, my group had to organise a charity bake sale.'
2. Task: explain your responsibility, 'I was asked to manage the budget.'
3. Action: describe what you did, step by step, using 'I', 'I made a list of costs, set prices and tracked sales daily.'
4. Result: share the outcome and the lesson: 'We raised 40,000 naira, 20 per cent above our target, and I learned to track numbers early.'
The situation: Dami is interviewed for a volunteer role at a children's hospital. The panel asks, 'Tell us about a time you solved a problem.'
How it often goes wrong: Dami says, 'I am good at solving problems, I always try my best,' and gives no example. The panel is not convinced.

b: Situation: 'When my class library had too few books...'
Task: 'I wanted to build a collection of 100 books in a term.'
Action: 'I asked neighbours to donate, set up a collection box at the church and posted a list on WhatsApp.'
Result: 'We collected 130 books, and I learned that asking directly works.' He then asks, 'How do volunteers get supported in their first month?'

p: Mistake: vague answers without examples. Fix: Use STAR stories.
Mistake: arriving unprepared about the organisation. Fix: Research its mission, values and recent news.
Mistake: no questions at the end. Fix: Prepare two questions.
(5 min) Choose three experiences and outline each in STAR form
(10 min) Practise answering common questions in pairs; the interviewer notes strengths
(10 min) Practise your first impression: greeting, handshake or smile, and a 30-second 'tell me about yourself'
(5 min) Swap roles and compare feedback
What are my three best stories and what do they show?
How do I feel before interviews, and what helps?
What questions would help me learn about an organisation?
• Preparation reduces nerves
• STAR makes answers concrete
• Good questions show interest

units.title: Week 45: Professional Etiquette
units.summary: Show professionalism in your emails, meetings, messages, dress and behaviour.

p: By the end of this unit you will be able to:
• Write a clear professional email with a subject line, greeting, message and sign-off
• Apply basic meeting etiquette: punctuality, preparation and respect
• Choose appropriate dress, tone and language for different settings
What's the difference between a text to a friend and an email to someone important?

sections.h: True story: Gabriel Santos (16 years old) (Manila, Philippines)
p: Gabriel Santos secured a great opportunity to complete a two-week work experience program at a large corporate bank office in Manila. On his very first day, Gabriel made a series of major social blunders because he did not understand the basic rules of professional etiquette. He arrived at the office ten minutes late wearing a wrinkled graphic t-shirt, sat slouched at his desk with his headphones around his neck, and sent an email to his department manager using casual text-message slang and emojis. His manager looked highly unimpressed and asked Gabriel to step into her office for a serious talk.

His manager explained that while casual behavior was totally fine at home or with high school friends, the professional world required a high standard of respect, punctuality, and clear boundaries. Gabriel felt deeply ashamed and realized that his sloppy habits were making him look lazy and disrespectful, even though he was a bright student. He made a firm decision to treat the remaining days of his work program as a lesson in professional behavior, changing his habits immediately to show his true potential.

The next morning, Gabriel arrived at the office twenty minutes early, dressed in a perfectly clean, ironed collared shirt with his hair neatly combed. Whenever a senior colleague entered the room, he stood up straight, greeted them politely with their proper titles, and removed his headphones completely to show he was fully present. When sending emails, he used a clear subject line, started with a formal greeting, and ended with a polite closing signature, making sure to double-check his text for spelling errors.

His sudden transformation amazed the office staff, and by the end of his two weeks, his manager wrote him a glowing recommendation letter for his future college applications. Gabriel proved to young people everywhere that professional etiquette is not about acting fake or losing your personality; it is about showing mutual respect, reliability, and discipline. He learned that mastering the rules of professional behavior is the ultimate way to build a trusted reputation and open massive doors for your future career.
What is the difference between a text to a friend and a professional email?
What is a professional habit you already have, and one you need to build?
Why do small things like punctuality matter so much professionally?

Professional etiquette is a set of habits that show respect for other people's time and trust. They are simple but powerful: arriving on time, replying promptly, using polite language and being prepared. People often decide in the first few minutes whether you are reliable, and these habits are how they decide.

Digital settings need the same care. A message to a teacher or employer is not a message to a friend: it needs a clear subject, a greeting, full sentences and a thank-you. A chat message that says only 'Hi' forces the other person to wait and guess; a clear message saves time and shows maturity.

b: Be on time, be prepared, be polite and be clear, in person and online.

sections.h: The method: On Time, Prepared, Polite, Clear
p: 1. On time: arrive 10 minutes early; if delayed, message early and apologise
2. Prepared: know the agenda, bring what you need and have questions ready
3. Polite: greet people, use names and titles, thank them and listen without interrupting
4. Clear: in emails use a subject line, greeting, one purpose, specific request and sign-off; dress and speak appropriately for the setting
The situation: Chiamaka needs to ask a company for a work-experience placement. She sends a WhatsApp voice note at midnight saying, 'Hello, I want to come and work for you.'
How it often goes wrong: She gets no reply because the message is unprofessional, unclear and sent at an odd hour.

b: Subject: Work experience request: Chiamaka Okafor, Year 11
Greeting and purpose: 'Dear Mr Bello, I am a Year 11 student at Greenfield School and I would like to ask about a two-week work-experience placement.'
Detail and request: 'I am interested in accounting and could attend from 3 to 14 June. May I send my CV?'
Close: 'Thank you for your time. Kind regards, Chiamaka.' She sends it during working hours.

p: Mistake: using slang and emojis in formal messages. Fix: Match the tone to the audience.
Mistake: 'Hi' with no content. Fix: Say who you are and why you are writing.
Mistake: ignoring replies. Fix: Respond within 24 hours.
(5 min) Rewrite a casual message into a professional email
(10 min) Role-play arriving at a meeting: introduction, handshake, small talk, agenda
(10 min) Practise a phone call to ask about an opportunity
(5 min) Discuss what to wear for three different settings
What first impression do I give in messages and in person?
Which etiquette habit would help me most right now?
Who models professionalism well, and what do they do?
• Etiquette builds trust
• Be clear and respectful in every message
• Prepare for meetings and calls

o: A clear subject line, greeting, purpose and sign-off
